I should like to ask the hon. member a question. We followed his progress

in Europe, and read with great interest a dispatch to the effect that he was victorious in an argument with the Russians. Could he tell us about that?	.

External Affairs
That approach was completely unrealistic for two reasons. In the first place, there on Formosa we have millions of people who, at the very least, are anti-communist. They are not in with the communists. Is Canada to take the position that these people can be handed over to the Chinese communists, to be shot by the thousand-turned over to be tried in these people's courts, these kangaroo courts, which have been in operation on the mainland in China since the Chinese communists took over there? Surely Canada does not propose to stand for a policy of that kind. Right Hon. Winston Churchill dealt with this point when he addressed the American congress. He said:
I am very glad that whatever diplomatic divergencies there may be from time to time about procedure, you do not allow the Chinese anti-communists on Formosa to be invaded and massacred from the mainland.
I suggest to the government in great seriousness that that is the policy which should be adopted by Canada.
Then the approach on the question of Formosa is unrealistic as well for another reason. That island must be held for strategic reasons. The line of defence on the Pacific runs from Alaska through the Aleutian islands, down to Japan, Formosa, and to the Philippines. Formosa is a key point in that whole line. With friendly air bases and naval bases in Formosa, in Japan and in the Philippines, it would be very difficult for the communists to attack this continent. That is the easiest way for us to prevent an attack on our own shores. If we give over Formosa to the communists, no matter what stripe they may be, then we are breaching that whole defence line, and the western coast of this country becomes the defence line.
It has been the policy of Canada for many decades that the best way to defend this country is to do our fighting as far away from our homeland as possible, and that is the obvious course to be followed with regard to Formosa. Therefore, I urge that Canada should take the stand that so far as she is concerned Formosa is not to be handed over to communists under any consideration. I repeat that our Secretary of State for External Affairs has no excuse whatever for a policy of leaving this question of Formosa "open", as he said.
Further, with regard to the Pacific, .1 am also disturbed at the minister's failure even to mention a defence pact in the Pacific. In the Atlantic we have this great plan, this North Atlantic Treaty Organization. In the Pacific there is no such arrangement. Obviously, something must be worked out. It is folly to leave the Pacific wide open.

The present policy in that area seems to be to have bilateral or trilateral agreements. For example, there is a bilateral agreement between the United States and Japan; another one between the United States and the Philippines; and a trilateral agreement between the United States, Australia and New Zealand. To none of these agreements is Canada a party, although we are a nation on the Pacific. Those particular treaties, at least the ones between the United States and the Philippines and between the United States, Australia and New Zealand, are designed primarily to protect those smaller nations against a resurgence of Japanese militarism. They are really designed as a protection against Japan, but it is a very interesting fact that both of them envisage a wider pact.
I have both treaties here, and in the agreement between the United States, Australia and New Zealand I find this paragraph in the recital:
Desiring further to strengthen their present efforts for collective defence for the preservation of peace and security pending-
And this is the important part:
-pending the development of a more comprehensive system of regional security in the Pacific area.
That paragraph is in the recital. Then, article VII of the treaty provides for the setting up of a council of the foreign ministers of these three countries, or their deputies, to consider methods of implementing the treaty. Article VIII gives, in detail, the hope that a broader treaty will emerge from this one. That article reads in this way:
Pending the development of a more comprehensive system of regional security in the Pacific area and the development by the United Nations of more effective means to maintain international peace and security, the council, established by article VII, is authorized to maintain a consultative relationship with states, regional organizations, associations of states or other authorities in the Pacific area in a position to further the purposes of this treaty and to contribute to the security of that area.
In checking up on the debates which have taken place in the United Kingdom and in Australia and New Zealand, I find that all of these countries are hoping for an extension of that particular treaty. They hope that it will develop into a Pacific defence pact.
Canada, I suggest, should now ask to become a party to the United States-Aus-tralia-New Zealand treaty. If there were to be trouble in the Pacific, if one of those sister nations of the commonwealth were to be attacked, Canada would be in fighting before twenty-four hours had passed. Surely it is the part of wisdom to make arrangements now, to get in now and work out plans together. Just think what a help it would be

to have Canada taking part in the deliberations of this council which is being set up under the treaty between United States, Australia and New Zealand. Such a treaty would serve also as a nucleus for a broader pact in the Pacific.
There is still time for Canada to act. I see no other way of putting an end to aggression in the Pacific than by setting up a defence pact of one kind or another. Frankly I cannot understand why Canada has hesitated to go into partnership in this area with her sister nations of Australia and New Zealand and with our good friend, the United States.
The second area about which I should like to make a few remarks is the Middle East.
I am very glad that the minister has been able to return to the house. I regret it was not possible for him to be here earlier. In the Middle East Canada is now vitally concerned, since Greece and Turkey have become members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Hon. members may not realize it, but under the North Atlantic treaty pact Canada is obliged to go to the assistance of Turkey if she should be attacked in her far eastern reaches. That is our obligation, an obligation which is new, and yet which was undertaken by this house at the session last fall. The result is that Canada is interested, vitally interested, in every thing that happens in the Middle East.
When he closes the debate I would ask the minister to explain where the government stands on two questions having to do with the Middle East. In the first place, what about the Suez canal? Do we agree with the stand taken by Mr. Churchill when he spoke to the United States congress just a few weeks ago or do we not? Here is what he said:
It is no longer for us alone to bear the whole burden of maintaining the freedom of the famous waterway of the Suez canal. That has become an international, rather than a national, responsibility.
He pointed out what a burden it was, and then said:
Britain is maintaining over 50,000 troops in the Suez canal zone, who again might be well employed elsewhere, not for national vainglory or selfseeking advantage, but in the common interests of all nations.
Mr. Churchill went on to ask that there be at least small forces from Great Britain's allies stationed in the Suez canal zone, and I may point out, Mr. Speaker, that half of the shipping going through the Suez canal now is United States shipping, made up largely of tankers carrying oil. Where does Canada stand on this question of the Suez canal, and where do we stand with regard to the Middle East command? Are we in favour
External Affairs
of a Middle East command being set up, and just what would be our attitude on that question?	i
My final subject is the British commonwealth. In his speech the other day, the minister made only one passing reference to the commonwealth. It is perfectly clear that he has no intention of relying on the commonwealth to preserve the peace of the world. It is perfectly clear too that he attaches little importance to the commonwealth as such for leadership through these dark days of tension. His attitude is in striking contrast to the attitude taken by the public men of the United Kingdom and of Australia and New Zealand in the debates in those countries on external affairs.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, the British commonwealth has come successfully through dire perils twice. Our peoples have been in terrible and serious troubles, twice within the memory of everyone in this chamber today.
I remember June, 1940, when France fell and Italy declared war on us. I remember our minister of defence, the late Hon. Norman Rogers, and the wonderful man he was, who was killed that very day in an air crash. I remember the terrible weight of tragedy that bore us down at that time, and when the British commonwealth stood alone for a whole year, and saved civilization. That took place about twelve years ago. The commonwealth was in both those wars from beginning to end, and is in a weakened condition today because of the efforts made for civilization in those wars.
In 1944 what was the position of the commonwealth? Here I have the report of a speech by Mr. Churchill delivered in Moscow on October 21, 1944, and I think it is of interest to the house. At that time he had a meeting with Premier Stalin, and here is an extract from the report of that meeting:
Mr. Churchill, over a microphone for Soviet reels, declared it his earnest belief that Russia, the British commonwealth-
He did not say the United Kingdom.
-and the United States would march in unison through years of peace.
These are the further words attributed to him in the report:
We have worked very hard.
Most of all has it been pleasant to me and an honour to have so many long and intimate talks with my friend and war comrade. Marshal Stalin.
I hope most earnestly and I believe with deep conviction that the warrior statesman at the head of Russia, through these years of storm and tempest, will bring his country into the sunlight of a broader and happier age for all, and with him in this task will march the British commonwealth of nations and the mighty United States of America.
It is only too sad that that wish has not been fulfilled. I suggest to the house, and

External Affairs
in particular to the minister, that right at this time the British commonwealth could be the greatest factor in bringing peace to this world. It joins east and west as no other group of nations can do. It must stand for peace, because it is vulnerable. It has had experience in world affairs, and it has patience, tolerance, understanding and judgment.
The Canadian government should realize this and should make every possible endeavour to strengthen the commonwealth. That could be done, for example, by Canada entering into a Pacific defence pact with Australia, New Zealand, the United States and possibly the United Kingdom. It could be done by Canada taking a stand beside the British on the question of the Suez. It could be done by switching many of our defence purchases to the commonwealth. We have an adverse balance of trade with the United States, a tremendously adverse balance because, for one reason, we are buying from that country practically all our defence equipment which comes from abroad. Let us switch every possible defence order to nations of the commonwealth.
It could be strengthened, again, by promoting migration from the United Kingdom, helping to disperse British industries in Canada, and to disperse British manpower. The industries crowded into that small island are subject to atomic attack, in the event of war, which would be disastrous not only to the British but to the whole of the civilized world.
We could take a full part in any conference held by the commonwealth. It is only a few months ago that there was a conference which dealt with Mediterranean defence problems. Canada, if you please, would not send its Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), but sent only one of the officials from the department. She would not sit in with the other British nations on an equal basis, although today we find ourselves obligated to fight to aid Turkey in the event of trouble at the far end of the Mediterranean.
Canada could strengthen trade within the commonwealth by stopping her attitude of' trying to persuade other British nations to cut down their preference. Let us stand behind them when they try to maintain those preferences which have meant so much to them and, incidentally, so much to many parts of Canada, including my own province of British Columbia.
And including the United States, too.

Then, again, why should we have this situation developing? Our Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) only a few weeks ago sat in on a conference of ministers of finance of the commonwealth. Now we find the charge being made by a responsible member of the British House of Commons, who was a former minister, that our Minister of Finance was a skeleton at the feast. Mr. Wilson said:
It was because at that conference there was a skeleton at the feast. I am referring to the Minister of Finance of Canada.
And this, I may say, was said on March 14. Then Mr. Wilson's remarks continued:
We are, of course, always glad to have the Canadian finance minister at any conference but it was his presence which prevented the Chancellor of the Exchequer from proposing outright discrimination against the dollar which is clearly what we ought to be doing at the present time.
I am interested in another way in which we can help strengthen the commonwealth. 1 refer to the Colombo plan. I was delighted to hear today a report on the progress being made in connection with that plan. I think the government is to be praised for what has been done, and I hope it will be possible to do much more. I cannot think of a finer way to win the lasting friendship of the Asiatic members of the commonwealth than by going all-out to further that Colombo plan.
There are many other things Canada could do. I have mentioned only a few of them. Probably Canada can do more at this time to strengthen the commonwealth than any other member-nation thereof. We might even be able to take a position of leadership.
This policy of strengthening the commonwealth is wise for Canada for the present, and it will be wise for the future. It would help to make Canada a great nation. Some people in this country seem to believe that the commonwealth is of no value to us, that we are merely helping others by continuing as a member. In that connection I should like to quote to them from a very interesting book which, I should imagine, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has read. I refer to the book "On Being Canadian", by Vincent Massey, our present Governor General. At page 100 we find this:
There are good reasons why the commonwealth is of importance to us in our national life; important both in our relations abroad and in our domestic affairs. For one thing, we have greater influence in the world as a member of the British family than would otherwise be ours. Membership gives us in a sense a double status. It provides one of the rare instances in which one can "eat one's cake and have it too." I feel sure from my own experience that the fact that Canada appears on the international scene, not only as an important country on her own account, but also as a member

of a great world association, lends her enhanced prestige. In the international world, prestige means influence.
I believe, too, that a policy of strengthening the commonwealth will not only help to make Canada one of the great nations of the world, but will help to ensure world peace, as perhaps nothing else we can do.
In conclusion, let us not write off the commonwealth, as many have been inclined to do. Great as the commonwealth has been in the past, I believe that under our young queen even greater days lie ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Lesage) upon the concise and, I think, satisfactory account he gave in the time he had available of what took place at the United Nations. I am sure he could have spent another hour telling us about incidents which happened there, and all would have been delighted to listen,
I found that our Canadian group at the United Nations held a place of high esteem in that organization, and that they have been doing an excellent job there on behalf of Canada. I do not intend to follow the arguments of the parliamentary assistant with respect to economic aid either under the Colombo plan or in the UN except to say that, like him, I see the difficulties that exist. But I do think that, even though those difficulties are there, probably we have to do more than we have been doing, to date. I feel that that is the objective of the government with regard to the East and the Far East.
Nor do I intend to follow the arguments of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) with respect to the commonwealth. I do not think there is anyone in the house who does not agree that the commonwealth not only has played but, in the future, will play an important part in the world of today. I think that is too obvious to need bolstering by arguments in the house.
However, there is one important subject with which I wish to deal. The impression seems to have been created in the house and in the country that, because we in this group agree that a position of strength must be attained if peace is to be maintained-or, should I say, if war is not to spread farther- we agree with the present government policy with respect to NATO.
I want to say, and as decidedly as I can, that this is not the case. While we do agree with the over-all objective, we certainly 55704-49
External Affairs
disagree with the methods by which this government is presently trying to implement that objective.
The minister of external affairs, in answer to a question of mine on page 672 of Hansard with respect to the amount of economic aid which Canada had contributed to NATO, stated as follows:
I cannot give any information in concrete terms as to what has been done in the field to which I just referred. Indeed, very little has been done In the field of non-military co-operation. I admit that, and I think we must all be disappointed that more has not been done.
He goes on to state further that feeling of co-operation that some progress has been made by the European countries themselves in the field of migration and the moving of labour between European countries, but so far as Canada is concerned the fact remains that nothing concrete has been done to date in connection with economic aid within NATO. In reply to a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as to what budgetary arrangements for carrying out the different economic proposals had been agreed upon, the minister stated and I quote:
There was a discussion of budgetary arrangements for NATO generally and there was an estimate made by the experts who worked with us on this committee as to how much these proposals would cost. They will cost a considerable amount. They include such items as exchanges of students and that kind of thing. But I am not in position to give exact figures in that regard at the present time. They will not cost much in relation, I might add. to our our total expense program.
I wonder if the government in thinking of economic aid thinks only in terms of a few students who might be brought to Canada. Much as that is desirable, I am sure that in terms of preparedness against any aggression in the immediate future it is a miserable contribution as far as Canada is concerned. The minister himself has stated time and again, in this house, over the radio and at international meetings, that economic aid must be made part of the defence of our free society and that military defence in itself is not enough.
It is now some three years since NATO was first organized. We are spending, not millions but billions of dollars on military defence, and rightly so, but the minister states that in concrete terms to date nothing has been spent by Canada as far as economic aid is concerned. He goes further than that and states that all that we have to show to date is a report of the committee of five which has been sent to the NATO council for their consideration and further reference back to the governments concerned for implementation.

External Affairs
Surely alter three years it is time that we had something concrete to show in this field which the minister himself admits is so important. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) in his speech the other day said that we must first have military preparedness to protect our investment in Europe in economic aid. Is that the government's position with regard to economic aid? I would ask the minister this: How can the European partners in NATO carry out their share of the military program under present conditions unless we in Canada are prepared to implement some of the pious statements which we have been making with regard to this matter? Surely one of the reasons why the European partners are unable to do more in the way of military defence than they have been able to do to date is a lack of raw materials and the prices they are having to pay for those raw materials to the North American partners in NATO. On February 1 the Montreal Gazette contained the following Canadian Press dispatch:
Mr. Abbott, just back from a second trip to Europe in recent weeks, said Canada couldn't approve a high-level NATO committee's suggestion that Canada send over free raw materials and basic commodities-copper, zinc, wheat-because it would imperil her own trading and economic position.
Later the dispatch states:
For that reason the finance minister said he was in full agreement with Mr. Pearson's statement that Canadian acceptance of such a suggestion would be "undesirable" in principle.
In other words, this government does not believe that we should make these essential materials available to our partners as a free gift, and on the other hand the government states by its actions that we cannot accept what Europe has in the way of goods that can be sold in our markets to pay for these materials. Just how does the government propose then to assist our European NATO partners in carrying out their share of the NATO program?
The whole basis of the C.C.F. argument with regard to NATO is that if NATO is to be successful there must be along with the military program a program of assistance which will enable every partner in the organization to do its full share. To build a military machine at the expense of the economic stability of Europe is to play directly into the hands of our enemies.
I was in Europe last winter and I sat in at the meeting of the French assembly when Mr. Faure formed his new government. That government lasted only five weeks and fell because it could not secure the necessary support for a money bill, the largest part of which was for the NATO program. What is happening in Europe? France has spent

over the past three years billions of dollars and the lives of countless hundreds of her best soldiers in Indo-China. We in Canada have been spared those sacrifices, yet our government refuses economic aid and the raw materials which are necessary for France to carry on. The same may be said of England, which has spent huge sums in Malaya. They have reduced and are reducing their standard of living while we in Canada want cash on the barrelhead for the necessary materials which they need in order to carry on an effective NATO program. On March 30, 1950, the hon, member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) asked the following question, and I quote from page 1376 of Hansard as follows:
1.	Have any Canadian loans or credits, extended to overseas nations since 1946, been wiped out?
2.	If so, what loans or credits, and in what amount?

1.	No.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
According to a Canadian Press report of March 16 in the Gazette the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), speaking at St. Michael's college in Toronto, said:
The foundations of combined strength we have already laid in the free world have given us a greater sense of security and grounds for hope that the war all decent people dread can be prevented.
I regret to say the precautions we have taken seem to have lulled some honest souls in our midst into a false sense of security, and to have induced them to join in agitation against the sacrifices and deprivations without which we cannot have any security.
As our hopes of keeping the peace rise, as our sense of security grows, we in the free world are facing the greatest test of our understanding, our resolution, and our patience. It is so easy to forget why we feel more secure and so easy to forget to pay the premiums on the insurance or even to ask ourselves whether we still need it.
I myself am convinced that if we are not to lose the security now coming within our grasp, we must be ready to keep up the insurance, much as I hope we may never have the fire.
WHat are we insuring against? We are insuring against aggression in the world, but that aggression is on two fronts, the military and the economic. The Prime Minister, according to the actions of this government, has taken out only one type of insurance policy to date, a policy against fire or military action. The government has failed, we believe, to recognize that there should also be a policy on the economic front. That is our objection to the present government policy. The government has put all its eggs in the one basket of military defence without making any comparable contribution toward economic aid, and the communists are making the most of that failure in order to promote

their line of propaganda throughout Europe. I might say that in many cases they are making a success of it.
Surely if the Prime Minister wants to insure against disaster, he should take out a policy that covers both of the dangers which threaten us at the present time. The minister of external affairs has on various occasions stated that the one danger is as great as the other; that we must give economic aid as well as military aid. Apparently he cannot sell that idea to his own government.
1 say that it is irresponsible for a minister in his position to make such statements unless he knows that he has the backing of the government in implementing them, and certainly the fact that for three years we have failed to do anything in this respect in NATO indicates something.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Does he consider that $300 million which is being voted in our estimates for mutual aid this year is an aid to our NATO partners?
The minister said in his own statement the other day that we had not done anything to date.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I never said that.

The minister is talking about mutual aid. We are asking that it be extended, not that the insurance be dropped.
The Prime Minister criticized those who join in objection to the sacrifices and deprivations without which we cannot have security. Let me point out that we are not complaining about the sacrifices. We are prepared to support greater sacrifices if need be. The leader of this group stated in the house on Wednesday, the 12th of March:
I would be prepared and my party would be prepared to support additional commitments for economic aid so that the peoples of Europe and Asia would be weaned away from the communist propaganda.
It is the attitude of the government in failing to extend the insurance to cover the risk which the minister of external affairs has repeatedly stated, that is the need for economic aid, that we criticize. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out, and the following words be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government has failed to take effective steps to achieve the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty."
Let me read to you what article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty states:
The parties will contribute towards the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by
55704-49J
External Affairs
bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and wellbeing. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
Perhaps I had better also read article 3:
In order more effectively to achieve the objectives of this treaty, the parties, separately and jointly, by means of continuous and effective self-help and mutual aid, will maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack.
You will note that in article 2 emphasis is on economic collaboration, and the putting into effect of better international economic policies and thereby promoting conditions of stability and well-being. Article 3 emphasizes mutual aid to maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack. I ask the minister of external affairs: what has Canada done to establish economic stability in Europe to date? Later I will indicate what the United States has done and is proposing to do in this matter.
In my opinion, Canada to date has made no real sacrifice to obtain greater security by paying some of the premiums of insurance about which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) talked in his address in Toronto. That may seem a strange statement, in view of the fact that we have a military program of some $5 billion over the next three years. But I want to point out the effect of that spending on the Canadian economy as outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in a speech to this house on March 14 when he dealt with the defence program. On page 436 of Hansard he stated:
I cannot think of a better way of summarizing the position than to say that we are taking the defence preparations in our stride. The expectation of acute shortages and of serious dislocations in the civilian sector arising from these defence preparations have not been realized. As has happened on many occasions in the past, the Canadian economy has shown once again that it is capable of a remarkable response to demands for adjustment and for a greater output. I do not believe that these reserves of economic potential' are by any means exhausted.
In closing his speech on that occasion he stated further:
National income and employment are at record levels. The Canadian dollar, without official support, has attained parity with the leading world currency. Canadians are prosperous and national savings are very high, in fact almost as high as in the peak years of world war II. There are some clouds on the horizon and I have no doubt that many difficulties will be encountered before the year is out. But, on the whole, the economic outlook for Canada in 1952 is favourable.
Let us compare that report with the report of Mr. Butler to the British House of Commons on. their economic position, or let us compare it with the economic position of

External Affairs
France or any other of our European partners in NATO. Let me quote you from a report in Keesing, on the economic condition of Europe:
A complete change in the position of many member countries in the European payments union occurred during the eleven months February-Dec-ember, 1951. France and Britain, which since the inception of the union had been consistent creditors, began to incur monthly deficits in April and May respectively: these continued throughout the period under review, turning their previous net cumulative credit positions into net deficits, and obliging Britain by October to start paying gold into the union.
And the minister states, our economy is buoyant and our currency at parity.
There has been some criticism with regard to what the United States has been doing. I want to say at once that they have been doing much more than we in Canada have attempted to do to date. ECA was started in the United States on April 3, 1948; the NATO agreement was entered into on April 4, 1949; the ECA program in the United States ended on December 1, 1951. During that period the United States gave to the world, not only to Europe, some $12,500 million in economic aid. During the same period, Canada gave not one cent to NATO. In fact, according to the questions to which I referred earlier as to whether we had cancelled any debts owing to us during this period, the answer was no. Not only did the United States give this aid, but we in Canada benefited directly as a result of it through offshore purchases of Canadian raw materials to the extent of $1,209 million.
Now, that is one of the reasons why our economy is so buoyant. We are riding on the other fellow's back. Since that form of aid by the United States ended, they brought in the mutual aid bill. I should like to give you a quotation from what the President of the United States said in his address to congress, as reported in the New York Times of March 7, 1952, when referring to the United States 1953 program. He said:
The funds required under the mutual security program fall into two broad categories.
The first of these, which is by far the larger, is for assistance in building up the military strength of friendly nations. This aid' is of two types:
(1)	direct military aid, primarily in the form of military equipment and components thereof, and
(2)	defence support-primarily in the farm of raw materials, commodities, and machinery-to enable other countries to sustain and increase their military efforts, where that type of support produces greater returns in military strength than would an equal amount of direct military aid.
The bulk of the direct military aid and of the defence support will go to strengthen the defences of the free nations in Europe. Amounts for direct military aid and defence support make up about 90 per cent of the total funds recommended for the mutual security program for the fiscal year 1953.

We do not know whether or not congress will pass that amount, but nevertheless those are the amounts recommended to congress. Of that sum they propose to spend a total of $5,889 million in Europe; $4,070 million for direct military aid and $1,819 million for defence support.
In commenting on that, the President had this to say:
To begin with, there is the contribution of straight military equipment and arms to help other nations defend themselves-and thereby help defend us. Of the funds I have asked for more than two-thirds of the total will go for these military items, because the largest gaps in the free world's strength at present are in the actual weapons needed for defence.
The second type of contribution consists of raw materials, commodities and machinery needed to support the military effort. For example, we might send steel to help another country make its own guns instead of sending it the finished weapons.
This is one example of what we call "defence support" for which I am asking $1,700 million.
Later he says this:
There is a third kind of contribution we are making to attain mutual security. There are parts of the world where plows can do a better job in maintaining stability and democracy than tanks or war planes or machine guns. There the communist makes his bid for power and not as a conqueror but in the guise of a friend offering an end to the torments of famine and disease.
I do not think, therefore, that we as Canadians are in any position to criticize anyone at the present time. Our economy is buoyant, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated, but it is buoyant because we have failed to take out any insurance on the economic front by making available to our partners under NATO any of the resources which we have except for "cash on the barrelhead".
The only group that I know of in Canada who have made any sacrifice in this line are the western Canadian wheat growers who have, for the last three years under the world wheat agreement, made one of the basic foods of the world available to Europe at a price from 30 to 40 cents below the price of class II wheat sold on the open market. I want to be quite frank in stating that the western wheat producer is getting a bit tired of being the only group in Canada who are prepared to make an economic sacrifice at this time. The producers of other raw materials that are needed, aluminum, copper, pulp, etc., are asking and getting all that the traffic will bear.
Surely if this government is honest in the statements made by the responsible ministers, that economic aid is as essential as military aid, they should be prepared to do more than they have done to date. In conclusion, I want to say this. If the Prime Minister feels that

there are some poor souls in Canada who are being deluded into a feeling of false security at this time, he had better look into his own cabinet and not across the floor of the house.

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) spoke he gave the views of this group on a number of points that had been raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he spoke in this debate. I merely intend to elaborate on a couple of points, namely the situation in Korea and the effect of the defence program upon the economy of Canada and that of other participating nations.
First of all, I should like to say a few words on the situation in Korea. I think great concern is felt in this country-and I found it also in the United States among those people to whom I spoke-with regard to the situation. By no stretch of the imagination can it be called a popular war. As a matter of fact, I did not meet one individual in the United States who did not feel that a mistake had been made when we intervened in Korea. As a matter of fact, they blamed the whole thing upon Truman. I suppose the Secretary of State for External Affairs will say that I must have been talking to Republicans. I may say, however, that as a matter of fact I was in one of the states that is represented by Democrats.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke, he outlined our objective in Korea in these words, as reported at page 665 of Hansard:
Certainly, all governments, and that includes the Canadian government, with forces in Korea, agree as to the desirability of bringing that war to an end as quickly as possible; but, as I have said before, on honourable terms which do not betray the purpose we had in intervening there in the first place. That purpose was-and remains-to defeat aggression there, nothing more. And we have not done that yet.
I would point out that before we intervened in Korea the objective was to set up a unified, independent, free government over the whole of Korea, both north and south. That was our objective before the aggression. I have always understood that after the aggression that still continued to be our objective. The resolution that was passed on October 7 in 1950 certainly made that declaration. The hon. member for Peace River quoted from that resolution but he left out what I consider to be one important clause in it. The resolution reads-
What are you quoting from?

I am quoting from the United Nations general assembly resolution that was
External Affairs
distributed amongst the delegation there. The resolution is headed "the Problem of the Independence of Korea". On page 2, it states as follows:
Recalling that the essential objective of the resolutions of the general assembly referred to above was the establishment of a unified, independent and democratic government of Korea . . .
It then goes on in various clauses, and I want to drop down to clause (d) because the hon. member for Peace River did not quote that one. Clause (d) reads as follows:
United Nations forces should not remain in any part of Korea otherwise than so far as necessary for achieving the objectives specified in subparagraphs (a) and (b) above.
What does paragraph (b) say? It says:
All constituent acts be taken, including the holding of elections, under the auspices of the United Nations, for the establishment of a unified, independent and democratic government in the sovereign state of Korea.
From that resolution one might gather that our forces will remain in Korea until such time as that objective has been achieved namely the setting up of a unified government over the whole of Korea and, if necessary, that those forces will be used for that purpose. I do not see how you can come to any other conclusion than that from the statement contained in the resolution. I would therefore say that our purpose is not merely to defeat aggression in Korea. That is merely a means to an end. The end is the setting up of that unified and free government.
On the other hand, am I wrong in that regard? That was the objective on October 7, 1950. Since that time have we changed our objective? Are we now giving consideration perhaps to the advisability of setting up once more two Koreas-north Korea and south Korea-with the 38th parallel between them? If we do that, I think we shall be betraying the people of Korea who have made great sacrifices up to the present time.
The minister stated that aggression anywhere should be met by collective resistance. On the other hand, however, he admits that it may not always be possible for the United Nations to meet aggression wherever it is committed because we have limitations to our strength. After all, the main danger spot today is Europe, and we cannot afford to dissipate our forces or spread them over too great an area, lest we may not be able to provide the defence forces which are essential in the defence of Europe. I agree entirely that our action in regard to the meeting of aggression is limited, and that we cannot probably hope to meet it at every point. But in my opinion, in deciding whether or not we shall meet an act of aggression or whether or not we shall intervene, careful

External Affairs
consideration should be given to the effect which that intervention will have upon the economy of the country against which the act of aggression has been committed.
For instance, let us take the example of Korea. We now know what the consequences of intervention have been to Korea. When this matter was first brought before the house during the special session, I think it was made quite clear by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that the North Koreans, in their attack, were being supported by red China and that therefore there was every reason to anticipate that during the course of the conflict there China would intervene. When I spoke at that time, I pointed out that the Prime Minister had stated that he hoped there would be peace within ten months but that in my opinion there would be no chance of peace within ten months unless China kept out of the war, and that there was no reason to think that once we started to defeat North Korea China would keep out of the war. Therefore, as I say, we surely went into that conflict with our eyes wide open, knowing that it might result in China's intervening.
What has been the cost of the war to date to the Koreans in South Korea? The cost has been ghastly, we know. Thousands upon thousands of civilians have died, partly as a result of enemy action, partly as a result of our own action, and partly as a result of starvation. It seems to me that to adopt the simple expedient of destroying the people in order to liberate them is a policy of idiocy. Perhaps that is the wrong word. I would say that it is a policy of brutality and that it cannot be justified. I suppose the Koreans will rejoice if a unified and independent government is finally set up, but I think many of them will consider that the cost has been altogether too high. I therefore say that in the future I think careful consideration should be given to the effect that an intervention will have upon the nation against which that act of aggression has been committed. The cost may be too high. I think the cost has been far too high with regard to Korea.
In this house we have had resolutions about such things as crime comics; but I wonder whether the crime comics ever did as much harm in this country as has the type of broadcast we have listened to with regard to Korea, about "operation killer", with reports about how we have dropped jelly bombs to burn out entire villages in South Korea in order to smoke out a few communist snipers. That kind of talk-and may I say that it is talk which I think should never have been allowed on the radio in the

first place, just to excite people-has caused a great deal of hostility to the operations in Korea. Maybe the reports were exaggerated. I hope that they were. I am afraid, however, that there is little reason to believe that they have been exaggerated because we have seen reports by different correspondents who have come back here and who have written lurid details with regard to what has taken place in that country.
I know that it has been argued, in support of intervention in Korea, that it will teach aggressors in the future that aggression does not pay; but I would say that it will teach the victim of aggression that intervention does not pay because the cost of intervention is too high. Whatever happens in Korea now, I hope that we shall not give up until we have reached that objective. The Koreans have already paid a tremendous price and it would be a ghastly affair if, after suffering as they have suffered and after having made the sacrifices which they have made, we were willing to accept any other objective than that of setting up a unified government over the whole of Korea. If the United Nations now settle for anything less than that, I would say that their prestige will suffer a blow from which it will probably never recover; and undoubtedly the North Koreans and the Chinese would look upon that event as a major victory for their forces because the thing which they seem to be most opposed to is allowing the United Nations to set up a government of the people's choice-although they no doubt think it will be of the United Nations' choice, it will be of the people's choice-over both North Korea and South Korea.
I turn now to the other question. The people in Canada, and I found the same in the United States of America, are very perturbed over the present international situation, because I think many of them feel this way. They know that when two major powers engage in an armament race the end is generally war. I think history records that. I might say the inevitable end of it is war. But, on the other hand, just so long as the U.S.S.R. have armaments far greater than our own, and so long as they continue to expand those arms, I believe we are bound to do the same. I cannot see any chance of doing otherwise. The main danger that I see is that if we do finally catch up and reach equality with the U.S.S.R. in armaments, then there may be a tendency on the part of some hothead to use some minor incident as an excuse to precipitate a war. That is the thing that I am most fearful of, even more so after being down in the states,

because there are many people down there who would actually precipitate a war today, because they think it is bound to come, and therefore we should act before Russia is any stronger. There is that danger. That is common knowledge. We have seen the expression published in the papers by certain prominent military individuals in that country.
I would say that the only chance of peace in the world today is for us to try to reach an understanding with the nations behind the iron curtain. I quite realize that that is easier said than done. It takes two parties to reach an understanding, and there is no indication at the present time that the other side is willing to reach an understanding on the question of disarmament. The main stumbling block seems to be the question of inspection. They do not trust an international commission to carry that out. It is unfortunate that that type of distrust should exist. I also feel that perhaps we are going a little bit too far in that regard. I recall that when I was at the UN two years ago it seemed to be the general policy of Canada and the U.S.A. to vote against everything that was submitted by the U.S.S.R., no matter how harmless the resolution might seem, no matter whether there appeared to be some merit in the resolution. We continued to vote against it on the principle that, as it was pointed out [DOT]to me, it was not so much what was contained in the resolution as the intent that was behind it. That may have been necessary, but I hope that if eventually we have any reason to believe there is a change of heart on the part of the communist world, and if they do really become sincere in their desire for peace, we will recognize that change and not say that it does not make any difference what is in the resolution, we know what it really means. That is a very dangerous attitude to take, and there has been quite a bit of criticism in Britain regarding the United States of America for being very very intolerant on that question and not being willing to compromise cn even minor points. I am not advocating that there should be compromise on major principles, but I think we could very well compromise on some minor points that would not affect the situation very much, but might help to create a little better feeling in the UN.
The hon. member for Peace River made it clear that we support NATO in its endeavour to build up collectively the defences of the nations of the western world, but at the same time he warned of the need to cushion the economies of those nations against the
External Affairs
impact of the defence program. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is all very well to talk about the desirability of negotiating through strength. On the other hand, we have got to realize that you cannot negotiate through strength unless your internal economy is also strong. Unfortunately, it would appear that the defence program which we have before us now may seriously undermine the economies of many of the member nations in Europe.
When the hon. member for Peace River spoke he quoted from the magazine U.S. News and World Report. I have another quotation that I should like to read. It is found in the statement made by I. F. Stone. I frankly admit there are many things written by this man that I do not agree with. The only reason I quote this statement is that it appeared in a New York paper on the 9th of this month and I agree with him entirely. The statement reads:
The U.S. needs that arms race as a form of pump-priming;
This is the statement that also appeared in the U.S. News and World Report. I go on:
. . . our output is so huge that the burden can be borne without serious decline in living standards. For western Europe the arms race is a luxury beyond its means.
In Britain, the arms program means the diversion of machines and metals from the export trades on which her imported bread and meat depend. Belgium, the one west European country to achieve recovery by orthodox "free enterprise" mechanisms, is being forced by the arms race into restrictionism.
I think all of us would agree with the statement that this great burden is not being spread evenly over the nations that are participating. I have no doubt that this program is helping to maintain United States employment, and the same thing may be said about Canada to some extent, because if peace came overnight we would have a serious problem in this country to fight unemployment. But that is not the situation in Europe; for every time they have to divert a certain amount of wealth to their defence program instead of to bread and meat, it means that some people there are going to have their standards of living reduced very greatly. In that regard I say, if we really are sincere about the need to build up our defence program, and build it up rapidly, we will have to spread that burden more evenly upon the people and nations that are participating in this defence program.
I had hoped that the parliamentary assistant to the minister would have said something about what we are going to do under article 2 of NATO to help those nations. I agree that the technical assistance program is a very fine one, but in proportion to the

External Affairs
magnitude of the problem it has not so far gone very far, and it will be of no immediate help to the nations of NATO in aiding them to cushion their economies against the defence project. It is not meant for that purpose, I will agree, but, as I say, it will be of very little immediate help to nations of NATO.
The point I am interested in is this. What does the Canadian government propose to do at the present time to meet the situation that I have referred to, namely, the need for helping those nations in NATO to cushion their economies against these great defence expenditures? I was quite concerned when I read a statement, apparently made by our Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in which he subscribed to the policy of helping Britain make sterling convertible. It was his opinion, apparently, that convertibility should be achieved just as rapidly as possible, and therefore he supported Britain and other nations in restricting their imports from the dollar area. In my opinion, if at a time like this when those nations are having tremendous difficulty in meeting their obligations under the defence program, on top of that we still further aggravate their problems by trying to insist that they restore convertibility, then we will be sabotaging the defence effort just in exactly the same way that we sabotaged our defence effort prior to 1939, when we permitted our industries to operate only 50 per cent of their capacity.
The reason I ask, what does the government propose to do in order to help the European nations cushion their economy, is that I consider there is a great deal that Canada can do without asking for any extra sacrifices on the part of the people of this country, because we can make a tremendous contribution to the people of Europe in the form of food without reducing the standard of living of any people in this country. I say that for the simple reason that at the present time farmers in Canada are actually being discouraged from increasing their production by officials of the government. In the face of the want that exists in the world today, when you have millions of people on the verge of starvation, when you see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) of this country suggesting to the farmers that it might be unwise for them to increase production because there would not be any market for it, then I say the government is not taking the steps that it could take to help cushion those economies.
I just want to quote, from the March 29 issue of Saturday Night, an article headed

"Back to Farm Surpluses and Canned Meat Market," written by Michael Barkway. I want to read two or three sections:
For nearly two weeks now, Canadian pork has been going into cans because there was nothing else to do with it.
At the beginning of March the available cold storage was full. Forty million pounds of pork were in store compared with about 15 million last year.
There was some talk of giving it away to Britain or to somebody else who needed it. But the emergency decision was to put it in cans.
No one knows how much pork will have to be canned. It will partly depend on how much Canadians eat this summer. But there will be millions of pounds of it-perhaps 60 or 70 million pounds. No one knows, either, where we may be able to sell it or at what price. One hopeful sign is that the U.S. spring crop of hogs is pretty low this year.
This is an interesting point. In face of the fact that millions of people are facing starvation in Europe, and European nations are having a hard job to maintain their economy in the face of defence programs, he rejoices in the fact, apparently, that there will be a poor crop of hogs in the United States this spring.
Now, what is the effect of this defence program on Great Britain? Again I wish to quote from Saturday Night, this time at page 4, where in an editorial headed "This Is Sterling's Crisis" it says:
It is a formidable thing to say, but this is the crisis of sterling. The Oxford dictionary defines this overworked word as meaning "the point in the progress of a disease when a change takes place which is decisive of recovery or death." Death can come quickly. Recovery is always slow and painful. We must be prepared for a long period of convalescence for sterling; premature rushes at convertibility will merely end in relapse. Canada must therefore adapt itself to several years during which the sterling countries will be able to buy only necessities from us.
Is that necessarily so? Are we not in a position to do something about it, so as to make it possible for European nations to get more food from us, or more food than is allowed under the restrictions they have imposed upon exports from dollar countries? Must we discourage the production of food in this country while, at the same time, that food is urgently needed in many parts of the world? I would say very definitely that that is not the case.
There are many ways and means by which we can encourage an increase in the production of food, and provide markets for it where it is most needed. And, just for fear someone may say that I am not making a fair statement when I say that the production of food has been discouraged in this country, let me quote briefly from a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture. I mentioned it in the speech I delivered during the debate

in reply to the speech from the throne. However, when I make a charge of that kind in the house, I believe I should produce the evidence at the time I make it.
I quote now from a speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture before commission I of the food and agriculture organization of November 23, 1951. At page 5 the minister said:
Our barley supplies are better than ever before, and our oat supplies above the long time average. These, together with our feed wheat position, make it possible to produce more meat and dairy products.
I am afraid this increased production of meat and dairy products will not materialize unless fears are removed from the minds of our farmers. The meat and dairy farmer has no assurance he could dispose of his surplus if it were produced. His experience suggests to him that there is no outlet.
And then in a statement he made before the Canadian Federation of Agriculture the minister said that-
-as long as Britain lacked the dollars to buy Canadian cheese and bacon and eggs he was not going to tell any farmer to produce more hogs, more eggs or more cheese.
When the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture commented on the speech by the Minister of Agriculture he said that, in view of that being the situation, farmers would be crazy to expand their production at this time.
Mind you, that was at the annual convention of the leading farm organizations in this country. That word will go right back into every part of the dominion. That word will go back, that it would not be wise for the farmers to expand production at this time, because there are no markets for it. Then, can anyone say that we are playing our full part in helping to feed the needy nations of the world? Are we playing our full part under article 2 of NATO? Are we playing our full part when it is frankly admitted that the defence program will make it difficult for some of the nations to maintain a satisfactory standard of living?
How can anyone make that claim, that we are playing our full part, when at the very time that this critical situation develops the Minister of Agriculture and the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture advise the farmers that it would not be wise to expand their production of food?
That is why I say that we could help under article 2 of NATO, and that we could do it without reducing the standard of living of the people in this country in any way. It could be done by increasing the production of agricultural produce, which would result in greater prosperity than we have at the present time.
External Affairs
That is a question I would like to hear the minister explain. I am not blaming him for this condition, because I realize it is government policy. But I do hope he will bring pressure upon the government to find ways and means by which the farmers can be encouraged to produce the food that is so urgently needed in many parts of the world today.
There is one thing we can never justify, and that is the curtailing of production of food in a time of actual physical want. We make fine declarations at the United Nations that never again will food be destroyed by man whilst there are hungry people. But if we allow this condition to exist in Canada, in the light of the condition disclosed before the United Nations, we are guilty of hypocrisy.
I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he speaks, to answer two questions:	First of all, are we
backing down on our objective to establish a unified and independent government in Korea and, secondly, what is the government going to do to encourage the production of food and make it available to the NATO nations?

Mr. Speaker, it is with a feeling of some diffidence that I rise to speak in this very important debate. First of all, I wish to make one or two comments about some of the speeches made this afternoon.
I always listen with keen attention to the speeches of the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I listened to him with particular attention when he was quoting an article written by a Canadian journalist who had visited the United States, indicating that he had found out that the American people were fully seized of the serious situation in the world, and in which he attempted to create the impression that the people of Canada are not familiar with it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am now speaking for the people whom I have the honour to represent; but I believe I can speak not only for myself, and my section of the country, but for Canada generally when I say that I believe the whole of Canada realizes the seriousness of the situation. But we have followed conduct similar to that we followed during two world wars:	We have kept our
heads high, because we have known that we have been doing our duty to civilization, freedom and democracy. The same principle applies with as great force today as it did during those two wars, in facing the present difficulties.
I am somewhat surprised by the amendment moved by the C.C.F., one which seems
778

External Affairs
to take a good deal of glory, or a measure of delight, in trying to belittle the efforts of Canada. It tries to leave the impression that since the close of the second war Canada has not played her part, or the part we should have played in helping in the rehabilitation of Europe and the rest of the world.
I know however that if their amendment were adopted they would be the first to criticize the government if, in implementing what they now request, taxes were raised again. What amount of money would they want Canada to spend on military defence? How many billions of dollars would they expect Canada to spend in helping to rehabilitate the rest of the world? I say they should be more definite in their statement.
We must realize that, since the close of the war, we have given a great deal of help. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has referred to the Marshall plan, and said that Canada had not contributed to it. We did not, and for a very good reason. The Marshall plan was an American plan. But at the same time we found it possible to help in many other ways the people of Europe and in other parts of the world.
For instance, without mentioning the Colombo plan, at the present time by way of mutual aid Canada is giving $200 million. Some people are thinking in terms of the Atlantic pact or the Pacific pact, in terms of millions of men in uniform, but they seem to forget that Canada has a population of only about 14 million. We have not 50 or 100 million people in this country. Our resources are not unlimited; they are to some extent limited.
I shall be interested to see how vigorously the opposition criticizes the government when it comes to the matter of taxation. The hon. member for Melfort tried to create the impression that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) wanted to create a spirit of over-optimism. The statement by the minister a few days ago was a very excellent one, indeed, and one which recognized-as it is recognized by other people-the heavy taxation we have in Canada. And we have that taxation, not only to implement our national services and to meet our national budget and military defence, but so that we may be able to help our friends in every way possible.
That is why I am going to vote against the amendment. Again I do not like the process of decrying Canada, particularly in the light of the fact that Great Britain, the United States and every other nation of the world which knows what we have accomplished do not hesitate to say what a fine part Canada

has played. We have received praise, and recognition too, for what we are doing at the present time.
There are Canadians who seem to take some pleasure in belittling our reputation, purely and simply for political reasons.
I do not wish to embarrass the Secretary of State for External Affairs but, in passing, I would point out that in my constituency we have a number of study groups who study national affairs, and the actions of the Department of External Affairs. I can tell the house that I am in a position to state that they admire the minister. They know that he has done and that he will continue to do a marvellous job.
He has received praise not only from the people of Canada but from people of every nation. Every nation of the world has seen this fine man in action. The minister has given of his great talent and of his time and energy to the work he is doing not only for Canada but for the cause of peace throughout the world. I say that sincerely-and I know he will realize I am speaking sincerely when I refer to this matter.
Those who belittle what he has been doing should keep in mind that people in other nations of the world recognize his qualities, and the fact that he is doing his full share. I repeat that, in speaking this afternoon, I am trying to voice the sentiments of the people I have the honour to represent. I am convinced that Canadians have very good judgment. Generally speaking, the Canadian people have good judgment. I always remember in our Liberal caucuses the late Mr. King used to tell us to listen and follow public opinion and we would never go astray. I have been trying to listen to public opinion as far as my own constituency is concerned and I find generally speaking they have only the highest praise for the accomplishments of Canada, nationally and internationally, and are proud of the fact that some very high and important positions were offered her.
I represent a pioneering section of this country. We do not do things up there in the easy way. The resources in that section of northern Ontario and northern Quebec are great but not unlimited, but we get along because of our energy, our strength, our work and our thrift. We are pushing ahead in this section of Canada and today northern Quebec and northern Ontario supports nearly 250,000 people who are making a good living there, which population was non-existent fifty years ago. Those people are realists. They do not keep their heads in the clouds all the time, but are realists and practical.

I remember during the last war the opposition was deploring the fact that we were not doing all that we possibly could. Some newspapers advocated that we should have at least one million men in Europe. Was that realistic? Was it not true that among all the nations that took part in the previous war Canada made one of the finest contributions in all departments? The same applies just as forcibly to the present situation. Canada is a member of the United Nations and through the United Nations we have made some commitments.
It is suggested by the economic and social council of the United Nations that as much as $19,000 million a year for an indefinite number of years be spent in developing resources in the underdeveloped countries. We will be part and parcel of that work whenever that policy is implemented. I am not going to prophesy, but I believe that as on previous occasions Canada will do her part.
The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) made a fine speech this afternoon and indicated the sentiments of the Canadian people about NATO. He did not speak as a partisan, and neither did the minister of external affairs. The positions they occupy are too responsible. They have too heavy an obligation and they cannot afford to do that. He told us very plainly that in the help we give to other nations we must consider their national aspirations and pride. We must endeavour to see that the money is distributed through the proper channels. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) would seem to indicate that we should disburse hundreds of millions of dollars to any government which may be in power at the time in some sections of Asia. Would that mean that proper help will be given to these people?
Let us be constructive when making statements of that kind. Let us be reasonable, not only with ourselves but with the people who are involved. As far as I am concerned, and I think as far as every member of parliament is concerned, we want poverty and need to disappear from the face of the earth if possible, but that will not be done in a day. This work will have to be done through certain national or regional agencies and it will have to be acceptable to the people themselves, always having in mind the respect of the people involved.
You only have to read in the papers what happened recently in the French Alps to show the deep attachment to the past. The government of France wanted to set up a hydroelectric development in the Alps, I believe, and it was necessary to move the people from 55704-50-J

The government had been trying for two years to get these people to move but they refuse because they are so deeply attached to then- own little pieces of ground which their ancestors have occupied for so many generations, and they had to be forced out of their homes, by the flooding waters of the project.
These are factors which absolutely must be considered in giving assistance to certain parts of the world. We know that it is more blessed to give than to receive, and in this connection we have that great generous nation, the United States, as an example. Through the Marshall plan it has done more to aid the world than any other nation in past history has ever done. Assistance under this plan was offered, not only to friendly nations but to Czechoslovakia and to Poland, both behind the iron curtain and many others. They were compelled to refuse by the U.S.S.R. Do you think for one single moment that the Marshall plan has always been well received or fully appreciated? No. On many occasions it brought unfair and bitter abuses on the giver.
These are all factors which as practical men and women we must consider before we go too far on that score, so that our help will accomplish its full purpose.
I well remember after world war I when my old mother country France was considered to be militaristic and did not receive the protection that was promised and Germany was considered to be the poor little nation that had to be saved from its financial difficulties. What happened? The United States and Great Britain poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Germany and then twenty years later she came close to conquering the world. These are factors we must be very careful about, and that are worth remembering.
I am quite in agreement with the Colombo plan. If $20 million or $25 million is not sufficient the government and parliament will provide all the necessary money. But how can Canada deal fully with countries having a total population of 450 million? Twenty-five million dollars would be only a beginning in offering them help. How far can we go on that score? We must try to achieve an equilibrium. These are all matters which of necessity we must consider thoroughly, and study from all angles.
I want to say a few words during this debate about the situation in Canada. Canada has never attempted to moralize to any other nation. Canada took part in two wars of which she was not an instigator. Those wars started on the continent of Europe where for so many generations and centuries wars have started and caused turmoil throughout not

only the countries of Europe but other sections of the world. We took part in those wars because we knew that we were on the side of freedom and democracy.
When peace came Canada indicated that she did not want any territorial aggrandizement or any maritime aggrandizement. All we wanted was peace to predominate among the nations of the world. In taking that attitude we gained the respect and gratitude of every nation. I say that deliberately. By that fact we were put in a position where, without dictating to other nations, without endeavouring to indicate the line of conduct they should follow, we could tell them about the seriousness of the situation. We could tell them how dangerous and explosive it is at the present time, and the necessity of honest compromises and of solidarity.
I believe it is the duty of the NATO countries of the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy and other nations of the world to endeavour to be friendly and to comprehend one another. I know it is impossible to have perfect unity in the world, since nations as well as individuals are apt to have differences. But if we honestly try to avoid friction between the nations we will be taking a real step toward peace in the world in our time.
There is a certain group in this House of Commons which at times likes to take a slap at the United States. I am not one of those. I consider it is fortunate for us that .ve are the neighbour of this big, powerful and generous nation. I am not going to emphasize that there are three thousand miles of unguarded border, but that is the fact. That fact is known to every citizen of the world. There is not a similar situation existing in any other place in the world. It is our bounden obligation as it is their bounden duty to have the good feelings between our two countries continue, to be continually cultivated and maintained.
Sometimes because of their great strength they do certain things, I will not say that we deplore but that we find hard to comprehend. For instance we are their best customer and yet for some incomprehensible reasons they have increased the tariff against us. However, when you take it as a whole the United States is not only a generous nation; by circumstances which are not of	its	creation it	hasbeen called upon to be	the	leader	of	thecivilized world. On this particular bill, No. 10, I am asked to decide whether the particular home which we are discussing shall or shall not be broken up.

I was interested in hearing-it was the first time I heard it-from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that the principals in this particular case come from our new province of Newfoundland. Evidently the people of Newfoundland are now going to adopt the same method of obtaining divorces as has been adopted previously by the province of Quebec.
I am not going to argue here tonight, sir, the desirability of divorce as such, or even the validity of divorce as such. I do not think that enters into the argument. I know that there are those who are totally and completely opposed to the whole principle of divorce. That is their right and that is their privilege. In certain cases they are prevented from condoning divorce because of religious convictions; and there is no one in the house who would not respect that particular course.
Then, sir, there are those who think that the grounds of divorce should be broadened. Constantly we see arguments to the effect that adultery should not be the only cause of divorce. There are even those who go so far as to say-and we number among them our American friends-that even incompatibility should be a cause for divorce.
As I said, I am not taking any position on that particular matter tonight. I .am taking a position with respect to this particular bill, and in respect of divorces which come to this House of Commons from the province of Quebec and the province of Newfoundland-and rightly so, under present arrangements, because up to the present time Quebec and Newfoundland have decided to have no divorce courts of their own.
May I reiterate once again that that is their privilege and their right. On the other hand the people from Quebec and Newfoundland are obtaining divorces, and they are obtaining those divorces through the facilities of this parliament. It is my contention that the facilities of parliament should not be employed for that purpose. I do not know the history of the time after confederation when these divorces were allowed to come to the house. But, sir, in those days they treated the matter with somewhat more seriousness than we do at the present time. The


other day I was digging among some old records-not in connection with this matter, but simply for my own amusement and instruction-which dealt with the earliest divorce cases following 1867. I wish I had that file on my desk this evening, because I noted in particular one case concerning one by the name of Martin, I believe it was, and I noted further that the case was before one of the houses at least in 1870 and that a decision had not been reached by 1873.
Let me say that if we considered in like manner the divorce cases now on the order paper, to say nothing of the hundreds which may follow, and if we spent three years on each one of them, then we might properly be accused of conducting something in the nature of a filibuster in the matter of divorce.
My point is that, as a member of parliament, I was not sent here to Ottawa by the people I represent to foe a divorce court judge in a divorce mill-into which this House of Commons has degenerated during the last few years.

I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but I think he is now speaking too generally about divorce. His remarks would be more appropriate in the debate of another bill now on the order paper.
