Looking at this bill, I wonder why it is here because, as I read it-and I am not going to read the names-it is an act for the relief of a lady, S.D.R. We are told that whereas the lady, S.D.R., residing at the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario, clerk, wife of C.A.R., who is domiciled in .Canada and at present residing at the city of Syracuse, in the state of New York, one of the United States of America, has by her petition
Private Bills-Divorce alleged that they were married on the sixteenth day of February, A.D. 1945, at a village, the name of which is given here, in the province of Newfoundland-and then it gives her maiden name, and the fact that she was a spinster, and that she alleges that the marriage should be dissolved on account of the only ground upon which a marriage can be dissolved in Canada.
I cannot understand why this case is here at all. Apparently the lady is domiciled in Toronto. It is my understanding that in Ontario there are courts to which, under such circumstances, aggrieved persons may apply to have their petitions properly investigated in the only way, in my opinion, that divorce cases should be investigated, and that is by a competent court of jurisdiction, where all the evidence can be properly heard and weighed, and a decision reached.
Here tonight we have a case about which no one in the house knows anything. We have a bill sponsored by an hon. member who, of necessity, because of his position as chairman of a parliamentary committee, has to sponsor the bill. I am not blaming him. But the bills are placed on the order paper, and in our hands, without one jot or tittle of evidence to indicate why we should grant this particular petition.
First of all I wish to relieve the hon. member, or any other member, from the responsibility; but I say it is an imposition to have this bill before us tonight without one jot or tittle of evidence that would enable us to judge the worth of the petition, and to pass upon it.
I cannot understand hon. gentlemen in the house proceeding to discuss the bill without knowing something about it. We are giving credence to the very thing that has been said of this parliament, that because of circumstances we are turning this House of Commons into a divorce mill. If ever there was a piece of evidence which would give credence to that idea, it is this bill before us tonight.
There is not one jot or tittle of evidence before us. The bill simply states that one party is domiciled in the city of Toronto, in the province of Ontario and is earning her living. The other known fact that we have before us is that the man in the case is domiciled in the city of Syracuse, state of New York, United States of America.
I am opposed to this bill, not because of the principle of divorce involved in it, although I might have some reservations regarding that matter, but because I do not think that this house is justified under any

circumstances in passing upon this bill before every hon. member has had an opportunity of seeing the evidence.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) tells me that the evidence in typed transcript form is in the possession of one of the officials of this house, but that is one copy only. I venture to say that not a single member sitting on the floor of this house, and this would include the sponsor of the bill-
Ask him.

-has had an opportunity to review the evidence. Perhaps the sponsor has, but if so then he is the only person in this house who has the moral right to cast a vote on this bill if he is satisfied that the petition is thoroughly justified.
I do not think we should be asked to pass upon a serious matter of this description without knowing exactly what we are doing. When the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) said that we were being called upon to break up a home that we knew nothing about, an hon. gentleman interjected to say that the home had already been broken up. That may be so, the home may have been broken up by one of the parties, but we should be satisfied that the home has been broken up so that the divorce may be granted legally and properly. I submit that that cannot be done until we have evidence to prove to us that we are justified in dealing with this matter and in voting upon it at the present time.
I am not going to go into the problem created by divorce because, as Mr. Speaker has indicated, there is a bill on the order paper which will enable us to discuss that matter properly and at length. Here we have an example of a petition in the form of a bill which is placed before us with not one jot or tittle of evidence. I say that no judge and no jury would come to a decision without hearing or seeing some evidence. It may be said that this matter has been before the Senate committee, but last year we worked it out that in most cases a relatively few minutes only could be given to each petition.
I doubt whether either of the persons involved in this bill appeared before the committee of the other place. I do not know whether the petitioner did, and we should see the evidence so that we would know. Was this case contested by the defendant? Did he come up from Syracuse to defend the case? Is this another of those cases where detectives were employed? Are we sure that we are not once again faced with collusion? There was no doubt about some of the cases that came before us last year and it was quite


evident that the evidence was false at times. How do we know that the evidence in this case is not as false as some of the evidence that came before us last year?
We know none of these things. I say to hon. members, for whom I have respect, that I do not think any of us dare put this bill through tonight without being satisfied that he is justified in doing so, without -being satisfied that the evidence is true, without being satisfied that there has been no collusion.
We took a new oath of allegiance the other day to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth. When we took that oath, what did we promise to do? We promised that we would faithfully perform our duties as members of this house. I say that one of the duties that we owe, not just to this couple here but to the people of Canada and to those who sent us here, is that before casting a vote on a bill of any sort, let alone a bill which destroys a home of two persons, one of whom is domiciled in Canada, we should be perfectly satisfied that in all conscience we can do this without any reservation whatever.
I am asking that, before I am called upon to cast a vote on this divorce bill, the evidence shall be placed before me so that I may have an opportunity of reviewing it. If I do not perform my duty-
What about your oath?

I was just going on to say that if I did not read the evidence, and voted, nevertheless, I would not be true to the oath which I took a short time ago. That would be a matter for my own conscience. But having this bill before us we should not vote upon it without seeing the evidence, without knowing everything about it. If we do so we are not fulfilling our functions as members of parliament nor are we carrying out the oath which we took such a short time ago.
I think this example is an indication of the correctness of the stand that we have taken on this whole matter of divorce. Divorce should not be a matter for final decision by the members of this house. It should be a matter for a properly constituted court of law. I have every confidence that no judge in any of our courts would grant a divorce based on a petition of this description simply setting out where these two persons live.

I think my hon. friend wants to be fair, but he says that no judge would grant a divorce on the evidence before him. He is not being asked tonight to grant a divorce on that evidence. There will be an

opportunity in committee when all the evidence will be presented. Then this bill will go before the private bills committee and come back here again. There will be three occasions to see the evidence.
As a matter of fact the hon. gentleman is incorrect. If we vote for this bill tonight we are voting for the principle of the bill which is the divorce of these two persons.
Which the sponsor said was so.
My hon. friend knows that when we vote on the principle of a bill we give tacit approval to the bill.
The hour for public and private bills having expired, the house will resume consideration of the business being considered at six o'clock.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Wright.

Mr. Speaker, in a little more than thirty-five years Canada has been called upon to participate in two world wars for which she was in no way responsible. At the present time we are deeply committed to NATO and defence of Europe which implies in the case of conflict that we would again pay tribute in the form of blood and suffering and resources on the part of our people.
As I said this afternoon, we should endeavour to get our friends the United States and the different countries in Europe to try to work together harmoniously. It is true that it is absolutely impossible to have no differences of any kind or no diverse opinions, but it should be possible in the present serious situation to try to get these countries to maintain in full their integrity and fine friendship, so that united actions will prevail. I spoke this afternoon of my great admiration for our cousins to the south of us, the great republic of the United States. In some quarters she has been accused of militarism, but this is an accusation that could not stand investigation. Has anyone ever seen in military history a nation who, after having vanquished her foes-some of them have been very wicked and have hurt the United States in her national pride-has offered aid through the Marshall plan? This aid was offered to every nation in Europe, but it is true that some of them could not accept its benefits because they were behind the iron curtain and had to listen to the voice and orders of Moscow.
External Affairs
In a few days this house will be called upon to deal with the Japanese peace treaty. Most of us have read that document now. Anyone who has read history must admit that he has never seen a treaty of the kind which the United States is offering to Japan. The United States was hurt deeply, yes, almost fatally, by Pearl Harbor, yet she is offering to the world one of the finest treaties ever given a nation to sign. This treaty includes some of the highest Christian principles, and I want to pay tribute to Mr. Dulles, the great American statesman who is the founder of that document.
The shift in world power was not desired by the United States. It has been, to some extent, imposed upon her. Her tremendous program for peace is an illustration of her sincere desire to maintain peace in the world. It is illustrated by her steady increase of the American forces in Europe, with no top limit fixed; a program of military aid to America's allies which this summer will far surpass the amount of Marshall aid which it may replace; two and a quarter years of universal military service on top of the present draft; a military three-year budget of $140 billion from July 1950 to June 1953, by which year her industrial remobilization will be complete; indefinite maintenance of the state of military preparedness thus attained.
These facts do not show any desire for domination. For nearly a century her actions have proved that she wanted to keep to herself. She wanted to be kept separate from anything that might happen in Europe, and the Monroe doctrine proves that. It is true that she was able to follow her destiny at peace because she had a wonderful shield in the British navy. At the same time, it was in her heart and in her soul to remain an American nation, working out its own destiny and not to be inveigled with what might happen in Europe.
If you do not want to believe my words about this, I shall quote the words of a very prominent newspaperman, Mr. Sebastian Haffner, as they appear in the London Observer. He said:
The rise of American power to overwhelming supremacy is bound to increase the importance of the United Nations, for the simple reason that America believes in the United Nations and bases her foreign policy on this.
America does not want to dominate the world; she does want the United Nations to dominate the world. She does want to see the charter respected and obeyed as world law, all nations acting in its spirit, and trespassers punished and forced back. This is what President Truman meant by the second part of his recent statement, when he defined the basic aims of American foreign policy in these words: "To see that the people in the

External Affairs
world have the things that are necessary to make life worth while, and that they live by the moral code in which we believe."
This may be idealism, and idealism as such may be a weak force in international politics. But idealism backed by overwhelming power must be taken seriously. The charter may well become the . Magna Charta of the second-class powers and the small nations in a world where, for the first time in history, there will be one nation stronger than all the rest together.
Now, that brings me to the question of Europe, and I want to discuss the question of the equilibrium of Europe and the equilibrium of the world. At the beginning of the twentieth century Europe could settle not only her own problems, but the moment that European problems were settled by the European nations they were not spread over the rest of the world. After world war I, I believe it was in 1920, the prime minister of France, Mr. Briand, said this:
If we have another war in Europe as serious and as grievous as the one we have had from 1914 to 1919, then Europe will become a world problem. Europe will not be able to localize these wars, they will spread as another world war and every nation may be involved. It may mean the end of European leadership.
That is the situation that is facing us. Today, we hope, we wish and we pray that the European powers will find it possible to comprehend one another as well as to comprehend the United States. Europe is facing two colossi, two great big nations, and the future of Europe might be decided on the knees of these colossi. It is very important for Europe to realize the seriousness of the situation. Let us never get away from the fact that if it is true to speak of the iron curtain in Europe, it applies just as forcibly to Americans, although geographically speaking they are located thousands of miles from Europe. On that score, then, it makes Americans, Canadians and Britishers and all the nations of the world realize that we are all in the same boat. Really, where danger exists for one of these nations, it exists for all of them. We must stand together, individually and collectively, or else we shall not be able to survive.
I should like to say one word about Great Britain. Sometimes she is criticized. I heard just one of the hon. members opposite say that Great Britain was bankrupt. I hope that this is not true. That cannot be true. Great Britain always had wonderful recuperative powers. It ill behooves any civilized nation to say that Great Britain will become bankrupt. For over a year during the last war she was the only human rampart against the hordes of barbarism. She paid a price in blood, in suffering and in devastation, greater than any nation has suffered in the world's

history. Great Britain is needed, just as the United States is needed. She has been a wonderful friend and a wonderful ally.
At the present time, I do not believe I could do better than to read-I do not like to read these excerpts, and I seldom do it. I believe this excerpt is worth while because, even in the United States, there is some inclination to make unfavourable criticism of Great Britain. I was deeply grieved when, prior to the visit of that great statesman, Winston Churchill, some newspapers in the United States and some congressmen were saying that Mr. Churchill was coming, hat in hand, so to speak, to beg for Great Britain. Mr. Churchill did not need to beg and he did not beg, while on this side of the Atlantic. Before the nations of the world, Great Britain is on our side. What are the assets Great Britain can bring to our cause? I quote from an article in the Christian Science Monitor of January 23, 1951:
Geographically, Britain is the sentinel, the advanced post, of the European continent. As a naval and air base she was vital in the second world war and would appear more so in an atomic war. She has national service of two years for British youth, and Britons are good soldiers . . .
The British empire, for all its reduced power, has a valuable string of naval bases around the world . . .
I am not going to read the whole of this editorial because these bases are known to all of us but the article concludes in this way:
The Briton as a human being has always been a sturdy, reliable friend and a tough foe. His courage and bulldog qualities have been shown innumerable times in history and never to better advantage than in that "finest hour" to which Winston Churchill gave expression and leadership. Such people are good to have as allies and much to be dreaded as enemies.
I want to make the same appeal as the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) did in his speech the other day. I hope it will be possible for men in public life in Great Britain and the United States to stop this filibustering against each other. Those things are not in order at the present time and could do a lot of harm.
I just want to say a few words about my old motherland. It was stated this afternoon that France is on the downgrade. I do not believe it. France, that generous nation, throughout all her history has shed her blood profusely for ideals and for principles, principles that are now practised in every section of the world. Many times she stood between tyranny and liberty. France may have her troubles today, but she will surmount those troubles as she always did. In considering France, we must remember what happened to her after world war I. Although she had guarantees from Great Britain-I believe this is the time to speak the truth-and from the

United States, she was left absolutely alone following world war I. She was invaded for the third time in eighty years, and at what cost? It will take me only a few minutes to tell you what it cost France in lives and in material losses.
Three times in less than one hundred years France was the first victim of barbaric attacks against the occidental civilization, under Bismarck, under the Kaiser and under Hitler. In 1870-71 France lost 156,000 dead, 500,000 wounded. We must remember those figures. In 1914-18 the war cost France almost a whole generation. She lost 1,427,000 dead on the battlefield, 700,000 invalidated, 2,344,000 wounded; 1 million houses were destroyed,
30,000	miles of road and 2,700,000 acres of forest and arable land were devastated. France has been hurt in her pride and is not in bankruptcy at all. France has her soul and her power yet. You have only to remember Verdun. Verdun is an episode that will show what she can do when she is fighting for her life. No greater heroism was ever shown than that shown by France on that occasion. What happened to France between 1939 and 1945? France lost 250,000 men killed in combat; 400,000 were wounded; 1,500,000 were made prisoners and 120,000 civilians were killed; 1 million children were killed or died from hunger and cold; and 250,000 men and women disappeared in concentration camps, in addition to the terrific material losses. Even though there is criticism of the policy of France, I feel that I am not making an appeal to deaf ears when I plead for her and say that France will show heroism in the future in surmounting her difficulties as she has always done in the past, when the honour of democracy was in danger, and the same call will be answered with valour and heroism.
We have great factors in Europe at the present time that are also satisfying to some extent. It is the great leadership given by its statesmen. I want to say one word about Germany. It is true that for centuries there were horrible wars between that nation and France, with no profit to those two great and fine nations. They both possess some wonderful qualities. If united they could bring marvellous factors and advancements in the whole civilization of Europe. The same thing applies forcibly because we have what we call a permanent union between England and France. Luckily for Europe and luckily for the civilized world ever since the bonne entente those two fine nations have been united together for many years and on two occasions it was possible for them to help save civilization. In Germany the time must have arrived for that dynamic nation which as
External Affairs
a people has wonderful qualities not only in the arts, and in music, but in construction, in engineering, in medicine. Surely they must realize that the time has now come that they must forget about their martial spirit and must now work hand in hand with the rest of the civilized world in saving civilization; to do otherwise would simply be suicidal.
Speaking of western Germany one cannot help mentioning the name of Chancellor Konrad Adenauer whose courage, statesmanship and vision have designated him as a pillar of Europe; and in being asked to sum up his hopes and misgivings as to progress in the negotiations on the Schuman plan and the European army, this is his answer and I quote:
These projects are not simple ends in themselves. They are also means to the positive end of a new. unified Europe from which fear, ambition and jealousy will have been banished. The goal of a European family, which will be the trustee and guardian of our common Christian civilization, is now within reach. We cannot afford to let slip the present opportunity of obtaining it for we may not get another opportunity like it.
On being asked if he thought the leaders of the other countries taking part in the deliberations see the matter in the same clear light, he replied without hesitation:
I know that they share the same view to a greater or lesser degree. There are points of differences and frictions; but they are largely technical. With a little patience and a spirit of compromise we shall have complete agreement.
I have been questioned several times about the feeling of other Germans. Outsiders seem to doubt, sometimes, whether our people are ready to honour the far-reaching arrangements that are being worked out in their name. I am often asked if they really believe in the European idea. I want to give an assurance that most of them can, and do, and will.
We recognized the statesmanship that Mr. Adenauer has given to western Germany just as Mr. de Gasperi, the premier of Italy, has given leadership to his country. These are all potentials which, if properly utilized, by trying to comprehend the mentality of these men and the difficulties they have to surmount and helping them as strongly as possible will lead to a united Europe.
Before I resume my seat, I want to speak briefly on a delicate but urgent subject. I want to praise the government, parliament and the Canadian people for having established some connection with Spain which I hope will be enlarged. Here in the house we sometimes hear people being called fascists, nazis and so on. Under the present circumstances, sometimes it might be well to forget some of the labels that might be thrown unjustly at some nations and at some people. As far as I am concerned, I am just as anti-communist as is any Canadian. But at the same time I know and we all

External Affairs
know the situation in Yugoslavia. While I know that communism is rampant, I would not criticize the help we are at present giving Yugoslavia because we believe-and
I	believe that we are right in that belief- that, being a friendly nation, we should not want to see her bow her head to Kussian imperialism although she maintains to a large extent a degree of communism. At the same time I believe we are warranted in being friendly with Yugoslavia, as she may also learn and eventually adopt our principles. On the other hand, why should we not be friendly with Spain? There is a tremendous military potential there. At the insurrection Moroccan troops fought for the liberation of communism in Spain. Let us not be scandalized about this factor. In world war I and world war II we had troops from North Africa and we had troops from Asia fighting to protect our civilization. No matter what we may think of Spain it is certain that the Spanish administration of that section of the North African continent proved that what they have done has been favourable to that population and they were glad to fight for the national integrity of Spain. No one will make me believe for one moment that any nation will fight more strenuously against communism than will Spain. There is a good reason for that, one that cost Spain a tremendous amount of blood and suffering. Let us remember what happened at the time of the insurrection about nineteen years ago. What was the alternative of Spain? If Spain had followed the line she was following then she would have fallen, like a ripe fruit, into the hands of communism led by Moscow; and the moment that communism became rampant in Spain, it could easily and rapidly have spread into every section of Europe.
I never discuss religious problems for the sake of discussion, but I remember speaking in the town of Timmins a few years ago-I believe that it was in 1941-during world war
II	at a meeting of protest held by my fine Jewish people with regard to the horrible holocaust that these people had suffered in Germany. I spoke at that meeting at which I was invited to be present; and this is what I told them. I said that as a Christian and a Catholic, when I hear there is persecution that happens in any section of the world-whether it is against the Jewish people or any other race or nationality, or against the Protestant or the Catholic faith-then I know that if persecution is unchecked it is bound to spread like a virus, a violent epidemic, and that there is something going wrong; and I am duty bound to protest because the primary tenet of your

faith, of my faith and of all faiths, is charity. The moment that persecution of religion is rampant, charity no longer exists.
What happened in Spain during the insurrection? Only a short fifteen years ago the church in Spain, one of the most glorious churches in Christianity, suffered tremendously in the way of lives lost. What happened there? Twelve bishops were killed; 12,000 priests and a number of the religious orders were massacred and 20,000 churches were devastated or burned.
Can anyone dare to say that Spain had to suffer those things unless it was done at the instance of the diabolical mind of communistic Russia? What harm were those churches doing to the Spanish nation or to any part of Spain or to anyone else in fact? What harm were those bishops doing to the Spanish nation or to the whole world? What harm were those priests doing or those members of those religious orders-some little sisters of the poor, some Christian brothers teaching the little children; some nuns looking after the old, the sick, the infirm. What harm were they doing or what politics were they playing? I will always remember vividly reading an article in the New York Times at the time of the insurrection. The correspondent there said that no one could make him believe that those holocausts were necessary; he said that no one could make him believe that it was necessary to destroy the Catholic churches in Spain. Why the killing of persons who were doing good work in the name of God? That is why I am speaking on that subject.
Again I repeat what I have said previously. Why the killing of persons who were doing good work in the name of God? Two years ago, when I saw that in Roumania the Protestant churches were being persecuted there, I took it upon myself to write personally in the best way possible to some agencies in the United States, hoping that my letter would reach Roumania, and to protest against that situation. One persecution always leads to another. Let us not get away from this fact. It is a virus, a pestilence that spreads itself in no time until everybody is affected and everybody will eventually suffer. I am just mentioning these facts because I hope and I pray that the authorities, whoever they happen to be, will personally make a special appeal to France at the present time to try to be more friendly towards Spain, towards its government and towards the Spanish people, because we need them at the present time. If you do not wish to take my words, you

may take those of somebody who is not of my faith and not of my nationality, someone who is not a Canadian, but an American. I will read to you an excerpt from an article written in the Reader's Digest of November, 1950, by William Hard and Andre Visson. This is what they have to say about manpower. I believe this is practical advice that they are giving to every one of us, because the sons of the Canadian mothers and Canadian fathers who are now in Korea and their sons and daughters who are in Germany at the present time may be called upon to engage in another holocaust, a ring of death on the European continent. Therefore they have the right to expect that cur government, all our friendly governments, the governments of democracies, will see to it that every factor is taken into consideration which will give us the best defence and strength possible against communism. I am going to quote the words of these two named gentlemen. They are Americans.
Similar remarks can be made in relation to Spain. Spain has an army of 400,000 men, organized into 18 divisions. These divisions need better weapons. But it would cost only one-third as much to ready these 18 Spanish divisions for war as it would cost to create 18 new British or French divisions.
The Spanish troops are violently anticommunist.
These are their words. I continue:
They would be utterly reliable on the German front against Russia. Why not ask Franco to put six divisions of them there? He would have a strong reason for doing so. If the Russians conquer western Europe, his life will not be worth many pesetas.
We all know that the communists do not like Franco, and to me it is an honour for Franco to be disliked by Moscow. He certainly must have done something against communism to be disliked', and he has never been liked since the Spanish civil war, because he stopped them short in Spain. The article goes on:
The argument against letting Franco help to thwart the Russians has been that Franco is a dictator. So is Stalin.
We worked with Stalin, and rightly so, during world war II. I do not criticize that because it was good policy at that time, as we thought that he would amend his ways.
He was our ally at that time.

The article goes on:
What is the matter with letting one dictator fight another dictator, if thereby he is promoting the ultimate triumph of democracies? The curbing of Stalin is more important that the ostracising of Franco.
Among some of the western allies there is a vigorous aversion to accepting troops from Franco.
External Affairs
Why is there an aversion? Somebody said: "Hear, hear". Who said "hear, hear"? I would like to have his name so it would be on the record. Why should1 there be "hear, hear" against Franco because he tried to save his own nation from devastation, from anarchy, from death, and who should be criticizing him on that score? May I put this question to you parliamentarians? What was the alternative during the insurrection? To let the communists run rampant in the peninsula so that eventually they would overrun the whole of Europe, or to allow Franco, who was and is a true Spaniard, to revive and to recuperate that nation from the hand of communism and from the hands of Moscow? I continue with the article:
The American reply might well be:
Very well, if you will not take six divisions from Franco to help save Europe from a totalitarianism infinitely worse than Franco's, why, then, you will surely not expect Americans to fill the gap thus caused. You will surely then raise six new additional divisions from among yourselves.
That is all I want to say on this matter. I thank the house for its kind attention. I know you realize that what I have said to you I have given in all sincerity, because I do not believe myself in persecution of any kind. I believe in the free play of all the people, in the true respect of all they profess and cherish no matter who they are, and I know you believe me when I make this appeal to you. When I hear of persecution of any race, of any religion, pagan or otherwise, then I know that in those nations something is absolutely wrong which should not be tolerated, and that we should see that it does not go on permanently, or else it will spread like wildfire.
Before resuming my seat I just want to bring a personal touch to what I have said. A few days ago I had the great honour of being re-appointed as a member of the standing committee on external affairs. I appreciate that honour, which carries with it some very heavy responsibilities, but they are pleasant ones to perform because of the fine co-operation and support that I have received from every member of that committee, no matter to which party they belonged.
I say to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) that I hope he will find it possible again, as in previous years, ever since the inception of the committee on external affairs, to act as our vice-chairman.
It is easy to work with you.

Thank you very much. He knows how much all the members of our committee and myself appreciate that. I

External Affairs
want to pay that compliment to every member of our committee for the fine work they have accomplished. There have been differences, but I am absolutely in favour of full discussion on any subject. This is the time and the place, and this is the machinery for that purpose. They have done it in the past and I know they will do it in the future. In the spirit of that co-operation it was possible to have, to a very large extent-I was going to say to the full extent-harmony so far as external affairs are concerned, and that has redounded to the honour of our country, our parliament and to the maintenance of peace throughout the world.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, in his statement on the international situation last Friday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) referred mainly to war and to preparations for war. The efforts of those whose duty it is to fashion our foreign policy therefore seem to have been diverted from the ultimate aim so eagerly desired by our people, namely the establishment of a sound and lasting peace, and to have been definitely directed towards armaments.
War is not unavoidable. But it is possible, and even probable, when nations rely more on might than on diplomacy to settle their present differences.
General MacArthur said recently at Jackson, Missouri:
(Text):
The United States administration is preparing us for a war in Europe after plunging the country unprepared into the Korean conflict.
(Translation):
Generals and military chiefs are worthy of our attention, because we call upon them to correct the blunders and the failures of the diplomats.
I do not question for one moment the ability or the devotion to duty of the present holder of the portfolio of external affairs. I even have confidence in those who assist him but I deeply regret the fact that our rulers, under the pressure of countries having special interests, have permitted themselves to be led into certain paths which can only lead to disasters even more terrible than those we have already suffered. Peace is a blessing from Heaven; we must be deserving of it, earn it through our sacrifices, our prayers and above all through observance of and regard for the divine teachings.
If the leaders of the nations of the world, in their meetings and their councils, would

give to God His rightful place; if, instead of sowing the seeds of discord, hatred and revenge through their speeches and the news papers in their pay, they would put into practice God's supreme command, "Love thy neighbour," there would be more peace and happiness on earth and the din of war would subside.

Peace cannot be ensured unless God reigns supreme in the universal order He has established and within the states...
. . . stated the Pope in his Christmas message of 1951.
Insecurity and terror are haunting the minds today. Where are the leaders who had promised to free us from this nightmare?
Where are the signatories of the Atlantic charter who had sworn to respect the right of all peoples to choose the political system under which they wanted to live? Where are the promoters of disarmament and cooperation?
Following the last conflict, a new world was to be created, putting aside God, His light and His precepts. He was banned from the United Nations. We are now faced with the results.
Where are we going to? The minister himself recognizes that it would be foolhardy to take an uncompromising attitude in such a changing world as ours.
We are carried on the turmoiled waters of communism, of unbelief and atheism. Stalin is at the helm and we are the sailors. We have forfeited a part of our sovereignty in favour of a supranational sovereignty which is subject to the whim of circumstances and to the dictates of the financial leaders interested in their oil enterprises or their munitions plants. We are fostering internationalism at the expense of patriotism. Meanwhile, Canadians shed their blood on the battlefields of Asia and mothers await in anxiety and grief the end of this useless massacre.
Why, I ask, are our troops not being brought back from Korea? What are we waiting for? Why do we not take our soldiers out of that hell? Are we waiting for complete extermination or the end of negotiations leading nowhere?

Time magazine, on March 17,	1952,
described the situation as follows under the heading "Purgatory":
(Text):
The dilly-dallying in the truce tents continued like drops of water in the old Chinese torture. It was eight months since the U.N. and communist negotiators had sat down to turn the war that is not a war into a peace that is not a peace.
On the U.N. side of the battle line, 450 thousand men-much of the cream of the U.S. military manpower-burrowed dismally into the Korean snow and mud, to wait for they knew not what. On the other side, 900 thousand of the enemy did the same. Occasionally, on either side, a man died-a bullet in the brain, a mutilating date with a mortar shell, a ride to earth in a jet-propelled funeral pyre. But the dying settled nothing.
In the truce tents at Panmunjom, nothing was settled either. A dismal pall of petty complexities had settled over a mission that once seemed pressing and simple. Daily, the truce delegates marched into their stove-warmed tents for the usual round of long, surly wrangles or ridiculous little meetings of a few minutes (one last week lasted only 120 seconds) at which neither side would speak.
(Translation):
The communists lead the dance. The negotiators journey back and forth. Lieutenant-General Matthew B. Ridgway, commander of the 8th American Army, said, as early as April, 1951:
(Text):
There is no end of the Korean war in sight unless a political settlement is reached elsewhere.
(Translation):
Following this observation the Ottawa Journal published, on the 10th of the same month, an editorial entitled:
(Text):
Now That MacArthur Is Silenced
It reads:
If General Kidgway be right-and red communist leaders have said that their objective is to drive us out of Korea-and we are unable to negotiate peace, or are unable to negotiate peace without appeasement or surrender, then what?
Some in authority tell us that our aim in Korea should be to "localize the fighting." But if it should happen, failing negotiation of the sort of peace we should want, that red China, determined to drive us from Korea, continues to mass against us overwhelming manpower, how long can "localized fighting" go on? Men cannot be expected to go on dying indefinitely just to "localize fighting." Our military position in Korea seems tragically unrealistic; bedevilled by confusion. We tell ourselves that we will not "reward aggression" (words of Mr. Truman and Mr. Attlee) that we will not make a peace of surrender. At the same time, and while the enemy is saying that we must either make a peace of surrender (he has scorned all other forms of peace offers) or quit Korea and continues to mass forces against us, we keep saying that we must not do anything in Korea that might induce this enemy to make "all-out" war on us; that we must not go beyond a certain line in Korea, and that we must not bomb the base and source of his attacks upon us.
All we must do is to see-saw up and down the South Korean peninsula in a war of attrition, using
External Affairs
such troops only as can be "safely thrown into the battle" and not even hoping (if we are to believe General Bidgway) for victory.
(Translation):
How far away we have drifted from the optimism and the enthusiasm displayed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who declared at the plenary session of the general assembly of the United Nations, on September 27, 1950.
Events-and United States and British soldiers- are rapidly demonstrating in Korea that aggression does not pay. It will soon be necessary for the United Nations to show, with equal vigour and resourcefulness, that it can deal with the problems of the post-aggression period in Korea. The political and economic life of that country must be established on a basis which will enable the Korean to fulfil the destiny that has been promised them. As hostilities draw to a close in Korea, and the assembly takes up its new responsibilities there, it seems to our delegation that certain specific principles should govern its decisions and that we should embody these principles at once in an assembly resolution.
In the first place, the general objective as we see it of the United Nations in Korea should be to fulfil the purposes which have been repeatedly stated at previous assemblies-a united Korea, a free Korea, a Korea which the Korean people themselves govern without interference from outside. This should be achieved by United Nations action and not through decisions reached by certain of its members.
There is no doubt about it, Canada has been in too much of a hurry to send its sons to Korea.
Of all the countries requested to assist the United States by far the greater number thought it better to stand aloof or to help out in a manner far more symbolic than effective.
For our part, says the Montreal St. John the Baptist society, we consider unusual, dangerous and provocative the zeal shown thus far by our leaders in Ottawa, who are once again resorting to the devices which have thrown us into two world wars. It is not up to Canada to take the initiative in forming an international army.
Faithful to its ideology, to its unshakeable tradition, our society is anxious to raise its protest above the hubbub of propaganda. It urges the utmost circumspection in the present emergency and protests against the idea of making Canada the policeman of humanity.
I am against war, Mr. Speaker, and against those who are leading us to a new slaughter.
Due to the present state of scientific discoveries, war is a destructive undertaking on a huge scale. The moment that the idea of atomic warfare is accepted, the idea of bacteriological warfare must also be accepted for the latter is not more horrible than the former but simply easier to wage and more dreadfully efficient. No one could say what would remain of the human race after a war in which new weapons of destruction would be used from one continent to another.
And, last but not least, it is untrue that a country or a group of countries-even the

External Affairs
North Atlantic community-has at its disposal sufficient superior means to be able to face war under good conditions.
Mr. Pierre Cot, a former French minister and deputy, wrote the following:
The truth of the matter is that under present conditions, the United States and its allies have an economic strength superior to that of their potential enemies. This superiority is temporary, but it exists and is important. But, if economic strength is the necessary basis for military strength it does not follow however that the relation between the military forces of two states or two groups of states is exactly the same as the relation between their capacities for economic production. Other elements must be taken into consideration, particularly the geographical position. The geographical position of the United States and their western allies is so markedly unfavourable that even if they still hold a margin of superiority in the economic field, it is much less sure that the situation is the same from the military point of view.

We fought from 1939 to 1945 in order to ensure the complete destruction of nazi tyranny. Those are the very words of Messrs. Roosevelt and Churchill.
We imposed on Germany an unconditional peace; we forced her to shut down her ammunition plants, while, after sham trials, our judges were passing death sentences on the nazi leaders; today, humbling ourselves at Germany's knees, we beseech her to rearm and we are willing to spend hundreds of millions in order to help her do so. I say that it would be the same thing all over again, should we one day defeat Russia.

In the meantime, the utmost is being done to spread everywhere a war psychosis.
On March 10, 1952, the Time magazine published an article entitled "Giant Strides". I quote from the article the following excerpt:
(Text):
A month after the Korean war began, General Eisenhower said: "You can't win anywhere if you don't win this one."
It is now apparent (see War in Asia) that the U.S. is not going to win the Korean war. Washington has not the will to win it. During eight months of truce negotiations, U.S. forces have grown weaker, the enemy stronger. There is no will to achieve anything more than a stalemate.
All Asia will note as a great new fact that the U.S. was unable to cope with the Chinese reds.
Europe, despite years of effort and the expenditure of billions of U.S. dollars, is still not defensible. France, drained by Indo-China, is in grave economic crisis. West Germany is still unarmed, still unable to defend itself against a Russian advance that might make a communist military spearhead out of German men and industry.
This is the background against which Secretary Acheson last week reported "giant strides" of progress at the Lisbon NATO conference. Such progress reports are familiar milestones of the last five years. They are true, in a way. The free world does move, but the question is whether that movement amounts to anything when measured by (1) the cost of the U.S. effort and (2) the progress of the enemy. Thus measured, the U.S. is taking "giant strides" north on a train that is moving south.
(Translation):
Canada, a powder monkey in the American galley, sails in the same direction.
The Prime Minister said in this house, on September 13, 1950:
But our present view is . . . that the most effective immediate contribution Canada can make to the joint strength in Europe of the North Atlantic nations, is the provision of arms and equipment, which will enable the young men of the nations of western Europe to have effective means of providing security for their own homelands, and of building up their combined strength as a deterrent to aggression from any quarter.
Why did we not stick to this wise and level-headed policy? What apparent or hidden powers have driven us to intensify our military effort?
On the other hand, I say that in leaving Spain out of the Atlantic community that now includes Greece and Turkey-countries that are in no way Atlantic nations-we made a political error which may be a fatal one.
May I now bring forward the testimony of Mr. Douglas Jerrold, a distinguished English historian, who said some time ago to the members of the Toronto Empire Club:
(Text):
Discussing the international cold-shouldering of Spain, Jerrold said its omission from the Atlantic pact was a grave error. The mistake was "strategic", because its geographical position gives it control of the Mediterranean, and any hostile power in Spain would dominate large parts of North Africa: tactical, because Spain represents the only really

valuable reserve of manpower; and political, because it imparts an unsound principle of doctrinaire political discrimination which, if persisted in, must prevent any effective European unity.
And later on:
We cannot possibly defend Europe unless all the nations are united. As long as different nations feel they will be subject to a political censorship, there can be no unity and this parts a fatal condition of division.
(Translation):
Canada was one of the 16 countries that abstained from voting at |Lake Success upon the repeal of the motion passed in 1946 against Spain.
It is unbelievable that such a country as ours should take such an attitude. The Secretary of State for External Affairs should try to convince his colleagues of the Atlantic treaty countries that friendly relations with Spain are a must.
It is fitting to quote Franco's opinion on democracy, as he expressed it to an Italian newspaperman in 1950:
(Text) :
If it is a matter of modus vivendi between peoples, then no friendship or sincere understanding is possible without tolerance and mutual respect. Not all countries stand at the same level of material and intellectual development, nor are the characters and idiosyncracies of all peoples alike, nor their faith, history, or traditions. The attempt to unify the world on the basis of what one people considers most perfect is the most intolerable of imperialisms, imperialism over conscience. If a system is good or perfect in itself, it thereby contains enough power of attraction to make others copy it. To claim to know, from a distance of thousands of miles, what is best for other peoples, is absurd. There is a Latin proverb which says: "The madman in his own house knows more than the sane one in somebody else's."
This is still Mr. Franco speaking.
The American people are an over-simple people and one that is readily deceived. They accepted the fact that Stalin was next door to a saint; he was the great ally, we might call him America's boy friend.
Many hon. members said the same thing.
But today it suits political ends to represent Tito as a real value, in view of his apparent repudiation by Russia. Spain's great sin has lain in not being willing to hate Germany or Italy and in having kept herself outside the general hatred for five years. Now today Italy and Germany are helped and Spain is ill-treated. This is something no level-headed person can understand. No political arrangements of international character are possible upon a principle of inequality, of victors and vanquished, of founder-members, full members and outcasts.
(Translation):
We must not wait until it is too late. The government's duty is to foresee, especially in the field of external affairs.
When the Athenians were threatened by Philip of Macedon, Demosthenes said to them: "Athenians, we must not be led by events, we must prevent them." As a gen-

eral marches at the head of his troops so wise statesmen must march, if I may say so, at the head of events, so that they will not have to wait upon these to know how to act, but will act so as to bring about the events they desire.
Our leaders must, of necessity, work towards peace. It is ridiculous to believe that they will achieve that result by preparing for a new carnage.
To the warlike endeavours of the enemies of Christianity and liberty we must answer with a crusade of good will. To incendiary speeches we must give peaceful replies.
The fantastic amounts spent on weapons of war will not prevent the expansion of subversive doctrines throughout the world, but charity, when applied to the relationships of peoples all equal, all beloved and all protected by Providence, can work wonders.
Peace was promised to men of good will and not to warmongers and fomenters of international strife.

Mr. Speaker, I would be inclined to reply immediately to the remarks just made by the hon. member from Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) but I shall have an opportunity, during my speech, to discuss certain facts he has stated.
The arguments brought forward during this discussion show how difficult it is for a government to follow a definite policy in view of the extremist views expressed on all sides. The Liberal party has once more chosen the best way to satisfy all these views when it decided on a middle-of-the-road policy, the policy followed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
I shall therefore have an opportunity to reply, during the course of my speech, to the arguments advanced by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Chicoutimi.
(Text):
Last fall I had the privilege of being a member of the Canadian delegation to the sixth general assembly of the United Nations in Paris. Therefore, I wish to immediately extend my personal thanks, and that of my electors, to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as well as to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), for having given me the opportunity to attend these interesting sessions. The hon. senator for Nipissing, along with the hon. members for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), Grey North (Mr. Bennett), and Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) were also part of the delegation. I am pleased to add that we had a splendid trip, and that a real, happy family spirit prevailed throughout the two months we spent together.
1 believe it would be appropriate to remark in passing that the practice, adopted by the government, of sending members of parliament from different sections of the country as delegates to the United Nations is an excellent one. It enables these members to observe at first hand the work which is accomplished at the United Nations-work in which they play an active part-and, accordingly, when they return home they have the advantage of being able to inform their fellow citizens through lectures or open forums of the various questions discussed at the United Nations. I wish to congratulate the government on its initiative, and only hope that this custom may be continued so that many of the members of this house may also enjoy the same privilege. I would also like to mention the courtesy extended to all of us during our stay in Paris by the leader of our delegation, the minister of external

affairs; I am quite sure that I am expressing here the appreciation of all the members of the delegation.
And now a word with regard to the advisers and all the personnel who worked with us during this assembly. I am pleased to say that they were competent and conscientious, at all times showing their willingness to work, and assist, even though the hour was late; they are deserving of our most sincere congratulations. While on this subject, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the house an article which appeared in Time magazine under date of November 26, 1951; it reads as follows:
In the brief time that the Paris meetings have been on, the Canadians have built a reputation as one of the hardest working delegations in the city.
I am reading this not because I was a member of the delegation, but because it is of interest to hon. members and the people of Canada. Often when the government sends a delegation outside this country one hears it said, especially if the destination is Paris, that this is a kind of picnic. I know that none of the members of the house say these things, but one hears such reflections. The article written for this magazine shows clearly that all the members of the delegation, whether they be Progressive Conservative, C.C.F. or Social Credit, are doing their share of the work. I continue to quote from the article:
They are housed in the small, dignified Hotel Raphael, only five minutes away from the United Nations headquarters in the Palais de Chaillot. The hotel's sixth floor has been turned into offices, where a briefing session is held promptly at 9.30 each morning before the all day United Nations meetings begin. Homework keeps the Hotel Raphael lights burning late into the night. "Don't ask me about Paris night life," said a Canadian delegate. "What are those Montmartre nightclubs they talk about?"
I have just stated my reason for wanting to put this article on Hansard.
In the course of the few remarks that I wish to make, it is not my intention to speak on the most important political questions before the assembly, because, after two months' participation at this meeting, one will easily understand that a member does not become an expert on international affairs. Moreover, all of these matters have been discussed in detail by the minister of external affairs, and by his parliamentary assistant. I would then limit my comments to the most important issues discussed in those committees on which I had the privilege to sit, namely, the committee on economics and financial questions and the budget, committees Nos. 2 and 5.

(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, as most speeches, except that of my hon. friend from Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) were made in English, I would like to go on with my comments in French.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the second committee deals with economic problems, which makes it one of the most important organizations of the United Nations, after the political committee.
Several questions were submitted to its attention, but the most important matter was doubtless that which concerned the economic development of backward countries. I would like to mention briefly two aspects of the question, that is, technical assistance and financial aid in view of the economic development of those countries.
It will be recalled that in 1950, the secretary general set up a technical assistance administration, which is part of the secretariat; in September 1950, Dr. H. L. Keenleyside, former Canadian deputy minister of resources and development, was made its director general.
I shall not linger to define the aims of that organization nor its operations, as its title is explicit enough and the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs already gave us a splendid report on the matter.
However, I would like to add that during the debates of the committee, I heard this plan spoken of in most glowing terms, by the very countries which had profited by it. Supporting their assertions by proof, the various delegates told of the numerous advantages they derived from the functioning of that body; they expressed the wish that it should carry on for a long time yet its beneficial activities, while improving its work. Fifty members voted for the motion moved by the United States delegation and seconded by the Israeli delegation; none voted against, while ten countries did not vote at all; most of them belonged to the Soviet bloc. The resolution supported the recommendations put forward in this field, for 1952, by the economic and social council, during its last session. In the course of the proceedings, the Canadian delegation said how happy it was to see that this program had been so successful and voted in favour of the motion.
Another resolution introduced by the Israeli and Haiti delegations, to send teams of workers and technicians from underdeveloped countries to study the industries of industrialized countries, was also passed, by a vote of 40 for and none against; but there again,
External Affairs
it should be noted, the soviet group abstained. In this respect I might point out to the house that in the course of conversations with several delegates from underdeveloped countries, I was told that one cause for complaint in those areas was the lack of experienced workers and technicians which seriously hinders the development of their natural resources and of certain industries which could be established there. That confirmed the soundness of my opinion regarding that plan and I congratulate the government of Canada for having, again this year, contributed an amount of $850,000 to this agency's funds.
The most important matter that was discussed by the second committee, during the first part of that session, dealt with the financial aid to be given for the economic development of underdeveloped countries.
On that issue the commission divided into three groups. The first group, which comprised the Central and Latin American countries supported by the Arab countries and most of the Far East countries proposed, in their resolution, that the United Nations establish an international agency for development which would be able to give grants for economic development.
The second group, made up of the industrial countries of western Europe and of North America including Canada, although they recognized the importance of that problem and considered it with much sympathy since they admitted the principle of assisting in the economic development, was compelled to oppose that resolution particularly because of the heavy burden they have to bear as a result of their own defence programs. The United States, which, evidently, were to pour the greatest amount of money into that fund, also claimed that many organizations were already functioning, that in particular they were implementing the so-called Point Four of their foreign aid program through an organization, which had been created for the purpose of furthering the economic development of underprivileged countries, and that it would be ill-advised, for the time being 

I insist on the expression "for the time being" because the policy may change-to create too many organizations for the same purpose.
The third group, made up of the members of the soviet bloc, abstained from voting and took the opportunity to renew its usual and well-worn attacks against the western powers, holding that the adoption of such a program would only add strength to the capitalist nations, which would thus better their own economy and prepare themselves to wage war.

External Affairs
The Canadian delegation also made a careful study of the problem of contributions. Everyone knows that it is quite a complicated matter that affords no easy solution.
It is generally agreed that contributions are based on a system similar to our own income tax system, that is on the ability to pay. However, it is not always easy to apply that principle on the basis of a strict mathematical formula and it often gives rise to political and technical difficulties. On the other hand, it has always been difficult to establish schedules of contributions both fair and equitable.
For the past few years the Canadian delegation had always strongly advocated a better allotment of UN expenses among its various members. This year our delegation has succeeded in having the committee of experts set up to establish the schedules of contributions approve the recommendations of the House of Commons committee on external affairs, which were contained in the report submitted to the house on March 14, 1951 by its chairman, the member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). This recommendation was as follows:
Your committee recommends also that Canadian delegations taking part in future in the meetings of the United Nations continue to insist that contributions by the Soviet union and its associates correspond more closely to their ability to pay.
Indeed, the contribution of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, which amounted to 6-98 per cent, has been raised to 9-85 per cent, while the rates of contribution of other countries in eastern Europe were also changed. On the other hand, the contribution of the United States was lowered from 38-92 to 36-90 per cent.
It was only after some lively discussions that these various rates of contribution were agreed upon, firstly because the soviet delegation, having pointed out the fact that its country had suffered a great deal of damage during the war, claimed it was not to be called upon to contribute more at the time. However, basing its action on the statements of several of their representatives who were boasting that their economic position was most brilliant and better than that of the democratic countries at the present time, the committee decided to override their objections. On the other hand the American delegation strongly opposed this scale of contribution, insisting that the committee apply immediately the terms of the resolution passed by the assembly in 1948, which stipu-

lated that, normally, no country should pay more than one-third of the total expenses of the United Nations. Nevertheless while admitting the importance of this argument, the committee decided that the time was not yet ripe to give effect to it.
For its part, the Canadian delegation exerted further pressure on the committee in order to seek acceptance, for next year, of another principle adopted by the assembly in 1948. According to this principle, it was recognized that under normal conditions the contribution of any one member could not be more per capita than that of the members paying the heaviest contribution. It will be recalled that this proposal had been agreed to at the time, on the Canadian delegation's insistence. Finally, the report of the contributions committee agreed to a resolution moved by Syria and the United Kingdom in which approval was sought of the contributions committee's report, it being specified that the principles adopted in 1948 should be applied as soon as possible. For the year 1952, Canada's contribution was set at 3-35 per cent.
There are other questions still, which have been studied by the fifth committee during that period; for instance, the suggestion of the American delegation, which has asked for the creation of a negotiation committee, comprising 11 members; it would canvass the various governments and collect voluntary contributions for all the United Nations specialized agencies. However, I shall not dwell at length on the other items on the agenda, for I have taken already quite enough time.
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, may I say that the United Nations Organization, although it is far from having achieved the purpose for which it was set up, accomplishes nevertheless some interesting work; our country has everything to gain by taking part in its deliberations and, in my opinion, must remain a member of that organization.
Before closing, I wish to say to the house that I was happy and proud as a Canadian to hear many other delegates from other countries say that Canada had an excellent reputation in the world, that we were privileged and had a bright and promising future.
I say once more, Mr. Speaker, that I was pleased to hear these words in praise of Canada because I am a Canadian and, if I may be allowed to say so, because I am a Liberal, since it can be deduced that those statements were made possible in great part by the healthy and wise way in which the Liberal party has governed Canada during

the past seventeen years, and since the fulfilling of its program will undoubtedly lead us to a future even brighter than the one forecast by eminent foreigners.

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was addressing the board of trade in Saint John, New Brunswick, he stated that external affairs were not held in private any more, that it was the business of everybody. I would like to remind him of the old proverb which says that everybody's business is nobody's business.
However, I think he deserves a good deal of credit for trying to get the people of this country to understand what is going on at the United Nations, and what the policy of Canada is at the present time. I must confess however that to me it is not so much what he says with which I disagree as with what he does not say. I find he goes so far, in his diplomatic way, and leaves a lot then to conj ecture.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has spoken on many occasions around the country. It is a wonder to me how he finds time to be able to do so, the time to prepare those wonderful speeches. If everyone read them they would certainly get a great deal of enlightenment. But it seems to me that rather than facts what we want in connection with foreign affairs is principles.
I remember when the United Nations was being founded in San Francisco I was in the United States at the time, and I have a clear recollection of the efforts being made by some delegation to have a dedication at the beginning of the proceedings asking Almighty God's blessing upon their deliberations. An objection was raised by Russia and, as a result of that objection, no reference was made to Almighty God. That should remind us of the expression that unless the Lord build the house they labour in vain that build it.
Since then there has been a great deal of confusion in all the discussions at the United Nations. The people of Canada, and I believe those of other countries, must find it very difficult to follow the affairs of the United Nations. I was down in the vault in this building the other day, at which time I saw hundreds of documents which came from the United Nations. I wonder if anyone knows the extent of the printing that is poured out from that organization, in connection with all the different subjects they consider. Until I saw that pile of documents I had no idea that the organization was so extensive as it is at 55704-51

the present time. I doubt whether many people know just how big is the job of the United Nations, or how big is the job of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I say we ought to be concerned with principles. Russia went to the United Nations in the first place as an ally, and has been turned into our greatest opponent. We no longer regard Russia as an ally. It will be recalled that in Mr. Winston Churchill's speech at Moscow he said that we and the U.S.S.R. were going to march forward after victory, together, in a finer and more prosperous world. Are we seeing that peaceful and prosperous world today, or are we seeing another example of the tower of Babel?
When the North Atlantic treaty countries met at Lisbon this year, and were welcomed by their host, what was one of the first things he pointed out to them? He said that Spain, a country of 28 million people, was not a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, nor is it a member of the United Nations. It seems to me there is a great deal of inconsistency in the attitude of the nations and ministers responsible for excluding Spain.
The leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who sits to my left, in recalling the discussion which took place in the committee on external affairs two years ago, reminded the minister that the announcement recently made that Russia wanted to balance seven of her recommendations against seven other states which were not communist, for entry into the United Nations, was discussed at that time, and that on that occasion both he and the minister seemed to consider that it was a reasonable proposal, that these communist states should be admitted, and that the other states that were anti-communist or non-communist should be also admitted. But I do not believe Spain was one of the states in the latter group.
What is wrong with Spain, that it is not even qualified either as non-communist or communist? It seems to me there is great inconsistency on the part of hon. members who are willing to take Roumania, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Russia, which are communist states today, states with communist governments, as members in the United Nations, while at the same time they are not willing to have Spain, which was one of the first countries, if not indeed the first, to raise its banner and to raise its forces to fight the spread of communism in Europe.
Why is Franco deemed to be such an outcast? Why are these 28 million people in Spain, a country with which Canada has had a long association in commerce, deemed to be unworthy to sit as members in the United

External Affairs
Nations or the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Are the people of this country familiar with the governments of Greece and Turkey, or sufficiently familiar to classify them as being democratic, or as being more democratic than that of Spain? Has either of those countries a better record for government, or a higher record in contributions to civilization than has Spain? On what grounds are they considered more useful members of the United Nations than Spain would be?
And, sir, if we leave the European scene, which most hon. gentlemen seem to consider a most vital part of the world-this unsettled and uneasy world of today-and go to the Far East, what do we find? It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) this afternoon that less than two years ago a document was published in which it was specifically stated that the aim of the United Nations was for a unified Korea.
All we want to do is put down aggression. I assume that by that the Secretary of State for External Affairs means the aggression of North Korea against South Korea. Perhaps he might tell me if I am right in that. He nods his head affirmatively. What about Chinese aggression? That is the aggression which has prevented the settling of the Korean dispute. The forces of the United Nations had advanced to the boundary between North Korea and Manchuria. The Chinese army, trained and I am sure equipped by the Russians, attacked and drove them back and we have suffered considerable loss of life and material since that time.
It seems to me that the aggression on the part of China is far more serious than that on the part of North Korea. I do not think North Korea had very much to say about it. They were egged and driven on and trained by the Russians for the particular purpose of attacking and conquering South Korea. But the Chinese situation is quite different.
Before I go any further perhaps I should congratulate the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) upon his speech the other day. I found it most interesting to listen to him, but I also found his speech rather provocative. I think he deserves some credit for giving a provocative speech because if it had not been so provocative I do not think I would have entered this debate. I do not know whether he should be given credit for that. However, he said some things which I feel require answering.
I remember that I interrupted him when he was speaking about China because he seemed to be saying things about China which seemed to be far from the actual facts. I do not

suppose either one of us has been in China, and certainly I have not. My contacts with Chinese have been few. I have a fair number of Chinese clients in my legal business. I know their general sentiments. But I have endeavoured to read something about China. I refer the hon. member to page 690 of Hansard of March 21, 1952, where he referred to Mr. Owen Lattimore. I remember reading articles by Mr. Owen Lattimore several years ago and I always put him down as a fellow traveller, even before I ever heard of Senator McCarthy. I certainly considered that he was to the left. Here is a passage in the hon. member's speech which aroused my objection:
Five years ago he warned his country that Chiang Kai-shek was out,-
Five years ago would be 1947. What inside information did Mr. Owen Lattimore have in 1947 that he could warn the United States that Chiang Kai-shek was out?
-that the Chinese people would have nothing further to do with him.
General Marshall said the same thing.

I am referring to Lattimore at the present moment. The hon. member went on:
Like General Marshall he said that they should endeavour to find democratic personnel in China and support that personnel in the formation of a government or failing that to endeavour to get a coalition government, which would perhaps have some communist representatives, that would prevent the country falling into the arms of the communist leaders in China.
With all due respect to the hon. member, he certainly did not take into account the recent history of European nations. Does the hon. gentleman remember a man named Mickolizyck who was brought to Moscow and threatened and cajoled into joining the Polish government with communists nominated by Stalin? He was threatened and cajoled by no less a person than Mr. Winston Churchill himself. Despite his protests, he joined that government. What became of him? He had to fly for his life. Did his joining that government prevent that country falling into the hands of the communists?
Does he remember Czechoslovakia, for which I am sure he must have great admiration. That was a liberal, democratic, artificial state created after the first world war. Does he remember what happened there? What was the recent history with regard to Masaryk and Benes and the rest of them? I am sure they must have a soft place in the heart of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Where are they today? Both of them are in their graves. One of them either committed suicide or was murdered and the other man

died of a broken heart when he saw his country gradually being taken over by the communists, the same communists whom my hon. friend has recommended Chiang Kai-shek should make an allegiance with?
No.
That is what you said.
That was General Marshall's recommendation.

Is it not a
rule of this house that if a member quotes somebody he is supposed to accept that as his own opinion? I took it that when my hon. friend quoted these gentlemen he was quoting them with approval.
I was quoting what he said at the time.
I suggested that the hon. member was quoting them with relish, not just with approval.
I did not notice any relish.

I doubt very much if the hon. member could rise in his place and justify that statement that he read us, whether he read it with relish or approval. My hon. friend begs the question, and he goes on to say:
Unfortunately support for the corrupt regime now in Formosa-
I question whether one, two or three men in a country of 450 million being corrupt would prove that the government was corrupt. I have read about Chiang Kai-shek and in his long career in public life, going back to his first association with Sun Yat-sen, during his twenty-five years in power, I have never read of his being accused personally of corruption.
Did the hon. member listen to the speech of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) who was in China for a long time with UNRRA?
I have spoken to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent and I must say that I do not agree with his opinion any more than I agree with the opinion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
He has been in China.

He has been there, but it is a great country. Other people have been there. I have not been there, but 55704-51J

I am going to read the opinions of people who have spent a long time there. The hon. member went on to say this, as reported on the next page:
Because of the fear of Soviet Imperialism the democratic powers have been supporting reactionary regimes like that of the Syngman Rhee in South Korea.
I do not know what my hon. friend means by that. Supposing there is a truce? Are we going to say to Syngman Rhee, "You have to get out, we are going to put in a government here just the same as we would have done if we had obtained power in China"? Are we going to tell him that is what we would have done if we had been listened to five years ago? Where would we get the power to pick out the right type of government?
Perhaps we should pick the hon. member for St. John's West.

Oh no; the
hon. member went on:
While we are not engaged in a war to put Syngman Rhee back in power-[DOT]
I do not know what we are engaged in; I am not sure that he knows.
-nonetheless there are elements among us who look upon that as a solution to the Korean situation. Then there is Chiang Kai-shek, and so on. The people of Asia are determined to throw off their bonds and we should be giving much more attention to this side of the problem than we have.
I do not know what side of the problem that is. Is that the sort of person who should toe governing the country when the war is over in Korea? Perhaps the hon. member will explain that later on.
Later on.

The hon.
member continues:
If there is any disillusionment among the Chinese people at the present time, and I think there may be, regarding their new communist rulers, we certainly cannot expect any support from the Chinese for the return of Chiang Kai-shek.
On motion of Mr. Browne (St. John's West) the debate was adjourned.
